teile.einleitung: In wartime many foods were scarce in Switzerland. So that everyone got enough, the state issued food ration cards. Only people with coupons were allowed to buy certain goods.
wichtigste: In the Second World War you needed food coupons to be allowed to buy food.
You still had to pay for the goods with money.
Rationed means: each person gets only a set amount.
From October 1942 bread was rationed too.
Heavy manual workers got larger portions.
Rationing was only completely over in July 1948.
There were already food ration cards in the First World War.

abschnitte.text: A **food ration card** had many small **coupons** printed on it. Each coupon stood for a certain amount of a product, for example sugar or butter. In the shop you handed in the coupon and could then buy the goods. But you still had to pay for them with **money**. The coupon only gave you permission to buy.

If a product is **rationed**, each person gets only a fixed share. This way what is scarce is shared out fairly. Without rationing, rich people might have bought everything up. Poor families would then have gone without. Rationing was meant to make sure that nobody had to go hungry.

In the **Second World War** Switzerland was surrounded by countries at war. Many goods could no longer be imported. Goods such as sugar were rationed early on. From July 1940 **bread** could no longer be sold fresh. Stale bread is eaten more slowly and in smaller amounts. In October **1942** bread also went onto the food ration card.

Not everyone got the same amount. People who did hard physical work needed more energy. So from 1942 **heavy manual workers** got larger portions. At the same time more vegetables, potatoes and grain were grown all over Switzerland. Fields even appeared in parks and on sports grounds. This campaign is called the **Anbauschlacht** (“battle for crops”) or the Wahlen Plan.

There were food ration cards as early as the **First World War**. From **1917** rice, sugar and then bread and flour were rationed. Later butter, cheese and milk were added. After the Second World War rationing was lifted step by step. In July **1948** it was completely over.

gewusst: Rationing in Switzerland continued for three years after the war ended.
From 1940 bread could not be sold fresh, so that people would eat less of it.

teile.einleitung: The Covenant of Sempach of 1393 was a common set of rules of war for the Confederate states. It laid down how warriors had to behave in the field. With it the states wanted to create order and prevent quarrels among themselves.
wichtigste: The Covenant of Sempach was concluded in 1393, a few years after the victories over the Habsburgs.
The eight states and the city of Solothurn signed it.
Plundering was allowed only with the permission of the captains.
Churches, monasteries and women who did not take part in the fighting were to be spared.
The booty was to be shared out in proportion and merchants were to be protected.
In 1394 the Twenty Years' Peace with Austria followed.

abschnitte.titel: After the victories over the Habsburgs
abschnitte.text: In 1386 the Confederates won at **Sempach** and in 1388 at Näfels over the Habsburgs. After that the states needed common rules for war. In 1393 they agreed on the **Covenant of Sempach**. It was signed by the **eight states** and the city of **Solothurn**. Solothurn was allied with Bern; it became a full state only in 1481.

The covenant laid down that warriors might plunder only with the permission of the **captains**. Disorderly plundering put an army in danger. **Churches and monasteries** were not to be attacked or robbed, not even in enemy territory. Women who took no part in the fighting were to be spared. That was an early rule to protect the defenceless.

The **spoils of war** were to be shared out in proportion among everyone. In this way people wanted to avoid quarrels among the allies. Only the authorities, that is, the **council** or the **Landsgemeinde** of a state, might ask for help in war. In this way wars begun on someone's own authority were to be prevented. The covenant also promised protection to **merchants**, because trade was vital for cities such as Zurich and Lucerne.

Shortly before the Covenant of Sempach, on 4 July 1393, **Zurich** alone made an alliance with Austria. After the fall of the pro-Austrian mayor **Rudolf Schön** it was dissolved again. After that all the states agreed on common rules. In 1394 the **Twenty Years' Peace** with Austria followed. Zurich was to vouch for the good behaviour of the inner states.

gewusst: The Covenant of Sempach was the first common set of rules that all eight old states agreed to.
So as early as 1393 there were rules to protect churches and uninvolved people in war.

teile.einleitung: The Battle of Sempach took place on 9 July 1386 in what is now the canton of Lucerne. There the Confederates defeated a Habsburg army, and Duke Leopold III lost his life. The battle is also famous for the legend of the hero Arnold Winkelried.
wichtigste: The Battle of Sempach was on 9 July 1386.
Sempach lies in the present-day canton of Lucerne on Lake Sempach.
On the Confederate side, Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden fought.
The Habsburg Duke Leopold III fell in the battle.
The Habsburg army numbered roughly 4,000 men.
Arnold Winkelried's heroic deed is not historically certain.
After the victory the power of the Habsburgs in the region was greatly weakened.

abschnitte.text: In the 14th century the **Habsburgs** owned a lot of land in present-day Switzerland. The city of Lucerne had allied itself with the forest cantons in 1332 and wanted to enlarge its territory. In doing so it took over Habsburg places and castles in the surrounding area. So Duke **Leopold III** of Austria marched against Lucerne with an army.

On 9 July 1386 the armies met at Sempach. On the Confederate side Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden fought. The Habsburg army was about 4,000 strong, many of them knights in heavy armour. After a hard fight the Confederates won, and Duke Leopold III fell together with many nobles.

According to tradition, **Arnold Winkelried** of Unterwalden is said to have grabbed several enemy lances and thrust them into his own chest. In this way he opened a gap in the enemy line. But he is only named in **chronicles** long after the battle. So his heroic deed is not historically certain.

After Sempach the power of the Habsburgs in the region was greatly weakened. Two years later, in 1388, the people of Glarus won the **Battle of Näfels** against the Habsburgs. Lucerne was then able to extend its territory further. This made the Confederation stronger and more self-confident.

At the site of the battle stands a **battle chapel**, where a commemoration is held every year. Many pictures and songs tell of the battle and of Winkelried. In Stans in Nidwalden a large monument has recalled Winkelried since 1865. In the 19th century Sempach became an important symbol of Swiss unity.

begriffe.erklaerung: A powerful noble family that came from Aargau and later ruled Austria.
A high noble title for a prince who rules over a large territory.
A history book in which events were written down in order.
A story about the past that is not certainly true.

gewusst: The Habsburgs originally come from what is now Switzerland; their ancestral castle, the Habsburg, stands in the canton of Aargau.
The legend of Winkelried only appears in written sources about a hundred years after the battle.

teile.einleitung: The Council of States is one of the two chambers of the Swiss Parliament in Bern. It represents the cantons, so every canton, whatever its size, has almost the same number of seats. Together with the National Council it passes the laws of Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Council of States represents the cantons.
It has 46 members and is also called the Small Chamber.
A canton such as Zurich or Uri has two councillors, while the former half-cantons have one seat each.
The Council of States and the National Council have the same rights.
The cantons decide for themselves how their councillors are elected.
When both councils meet together, it is called the United Federal Assembly, with 246 members.
In 1971 Lise Girardin was elected the first woman to the Council of States.

abschnitte.titel: What is the Council of States?
abschnitte.text: The Swiss Parliament is called the **Federal Assembly** and has two chambers: the National Council and the Council of States. The National Council represents the people, the Council of States the cantons, which used to be called the Stände (estates). Because it has only 46 members it is also called the **Small Chamber**. It has existed since the founding of the federal state in 1848.

Every canton has two seats, whether it is as big as Zurich or as small as Uri. The former **half-cantons** have only one seat: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel City, Basel Country, Appenzell Outer Rhodes and Appenzell Inner Rhodes. So 20 cantons with two seats each and 6 cantons with one seat each make 46 members. As a result small cantons carry great weight in the Council of States.

The cantons decide for themselves how their councillors are elected. Almost everywhere the **majority system** applies, in which the people with the most votes win. Only Jura and Neuchâtel elect by **proportional representation**, in which the seats are shared out according to the parties' share of the votes. The election usually takes place every four years together with the National Council elections.

The Council of States and the National Council have **equal rights**. A law applies only if both chambers agree. If they still disagree after three readings each, the **conciliation committee** is set up, in which members of both councils look for a compromise. Parliament normally meets four times a year for a three week session in the Federal Palace.

Sometimes both councils meet together in the National Council chamber. This is called the **United Federal Assembly**, with 246 members, that is, 200 National Councillors and 46 Councillors of States. It elects, for example, the members of the Federal Council and the federal judges. In times of war it also elects the General of the army.

abschnitte.titel: Women in the Council of States
abschnitte.text: Only since 1971 have women in Switzerland been allowed to vote and be elected at federal level. In the same year the Geneva woman **Lise Girardin** was elected the first woman to the Council of States. Today clearly more women sit in the Council of States than then. The Council of States is led each year by a different president.

begriffe.erklaerung: Part of a parliament that debates and votes on its own.
A way of electing in which the people with the most votes are elected.
A way of electing in which the seats are shared out according to the parties' share of the votes.
Former name for cantons that arose from the division of a canton.
The period in which Parliament meets and debates.

gewusst: A Councillor of States from Uri represents far fewer people than one from Zurich, but carries exactly the same weight.
The Council of States meets in a chamber of its own, a smaller one, in the Federal Palace in Bern.

teile.einleitung: Paracelsus was a doctor and natural scientist from Switzerland who lived in the 16th century. He questioned much of what the doctors of his time believed and looked for new ways to understand and cure illnesses.
wichtigste: Paracelsus was born around 1493 near Einsiedeln.
His father was also a doctor.
He travelled through many countries of Europe all his life.
In 1527 he became town physician and teacher in Basel.
He gave his lectures in German instead of Latin.
He made remedies from plants, metals and minerals.
He died in Salzburg in 1541.

abschnitte.text: Paracelsus was really called **Theophrastus Bombast von Hohenheim**. He was born around 1493 near **Einsiedeln** in what is now the canton of Schwyz. His father was a doctor and taught him a great deal about plants and medicine early on. Later the family moved to Villach in Carinthia, which is now part of Austria. There the young Theophrastus also got to know mining and working with metals. He gave himself the name “Paracelsus”.

Paracelsus rarely stayed long in one place. He travelled through many countries of Europe and worked as a doctor in many places. On the way he learned not only from learned doctors but also from **miners**, craftsmen and herbalists. He found that you learn more from experience than just from old books. He even wrote a separate work on the illnesses of miners.

In 1527 Paracelsus became **town physician** of Basel and was allowed to teach at the university. At that time professors almost always taught in **Latin**. Paracelsus, by contrast, spoke **German** so that more people could understand him. He sharply criticised the old teachings and often got into quarrels as a result. After a short time he had to leave Basel again.

Paracelsus made remedies not only from **plants** but also from **metals** and **minerals**. For this he used methods of alchemy, an early form of chemistry. This made him a pioneer: he combined medicine and chemistry. His teaching that almost any substance can be poisonous is famous. It depends on the amount. In short: **the dose makes the poison.**

Paracelsus died in **1541** in **Salzburg** and is buried there too. Many of his writings were only printed after his death. His ideas were controversial but inspired many later doctors and researchers. Today he is regarded as one of the most important doctors of his time.

gewusst: The saying “the dose makes the poison” is still quoted today in the study of poisons (toxicology).
Paracelsus sometimes signed with the additional name “Eremita” (hermit), which points to his origins in Einsiedeln.

teile.einleitung: In the Old Confederation the Tagsatzung, or Federal Diet, was the assembly of the envoys of the states. There they discussed common questions. It was not a government in today's sense, however.
wichtigste: Envoys of the Confederate states met at the Tagsatzung.
The envoys were bound by the instructions of their states.
The decisions were called Abschiede (recesses).
It often met in Baden, and from 1742 to 1797 in Frauenfeld.
The Vorort (leading state) led the assembly, usually Zurich.
Since 1513 there were 13 states.
In 1848 Parliament replaced the Tagsatzung.

abschnitte.text: The Old Confederation was an alliance of **states**, as the present-day cantons were then called. At the **Tagsatzung** their **envoys** met. They discussed common questions such as war, peace and the administration of the **subject territories**. The name comes from “setting a day”: people agreed a day for a negotiation. After Appenzell was taken in in 1513 there were 13 states, and that remained so until 1798.

The Tagsatzung could not simply give orders to the states. The envoys received exact **instructions** from their authorities. Important decisions applied only if the states agreed. So a question often had to be discussed at home and talked over further at a later Tagsatzung. The decisions and minutes were written down as **Abschiede**. The envoys took them home with them.

In the 15th and 16th centuries it met especially often in **Baden**. The town lay in a **Common Lordship**, which belonged to several states together, and was easy to reach. After the Second War of Villmergen Baden lost importance. From 1742 to 1797 **Frauenfeld** in Thurgau was the fixed meeting place. The **Vorort** had the right to invite and to lead, in the Old Confederation usually **Zurich**.

Besides the states there were **Associated States** such as the city of St Gallen or Valais. They were allies but did not have full rights at the Tagsatzung. After 1815 the Tagsatzung met again, now as an assembly of the 22 cantons. With the **Federal Constitution of 1848** it was abolished. In its place came Parliament with the **National Council** and the **Council of States**.

gewusst: The Abschiede of the Tagsatzung were collected and printed in the 19th century; they fill many thick volumes.
The word “Abschied” here did not mean “farewell” but what had been decided on parting.

teile.einleitung: On 9 April 1388 the people of **Glarus** defeated a Habsburg army at **Näfels**. In this way they secured their freedom. To this day the **Näfelser Fahrt** recalls this battle every year.
wichtigste: The Battle of Näfels took place on 9 April 1388.
The people of Glarus wanted to free themselves from Habsburg rule.
They were heavily outnumbered.
A few weeks earlier the garrison of Weesen had been attacked at night.
The people of Glarus threw stones and boulders at their opponents.
The Näfelser Fahrt takes place on the first Thursday in April.

abschnitte.text: The Glarus region was long under the rule of the **Habsburgs**. Since 1352 Glarus had been allied with the Confederates. After the Confederates' victory at **Sempach** in 1386, the people of Glarus wanted to free themselves completely. The Habsburgs wanted to prevent this. Näfels was the last great battle of this war.

abschnitte.titel: The Night of Murder at Weesen
abschnitte.text: A few weeks before the battle, in February 1388, something happened in **Weesen** on Lake Walen. Inhabitants secretly opened the gates to the Habsburgs. The Confederate **garrison** was attacked in the night, and most of the men were killed. This is called the **Night of Murder at Weesen**. From there an attack on Glarus was now threatened.

On **9 April 1388** a large Habsburg army marched into the Glarus region. The people of Glarus, with a few helpers from central Switzerland, were **heavily outnumbered**. From the slope they threw **stones and boulders** at the disordered army. Many of their opponents fled, and some drowned near Weesen as they ran. The people of Glarus **won**.

For centuries the **Näfelser Fahrt** has recalled the victory. Every year the people of Glarus walk to the **battle memorial**. There the names of the fallen are read out, and there are prayers and speeches. Because the battle took place on a **Thursday in April**, the **first Thursday in April** is a **public holiday** in the canton of Glarus.

gewusst: The Näfelser Fahrt is one of the most important holidays in the canton of Glarus and has been observed since the Middle Ages.
The patron saint of Glarus is Saint Fridolin, who can also be seen in the cantonal coat of arms.

teile.einleitung: Rudolf Brun was the first **mayor** of Zurich. In 1336, after a coup, he took power and gave the city a new constitution. This gave craftsmen a share in government for the first time.
wichtigste: Rudolf Brun became the first mayor of Zurich in 1336.
He was elected for life.
His guild constitution divided the craftsmen into 13 guilds.
The guild masters now sat on the council.
In 1350 an attack by the exiles failed, the Zurich Night of Murder.
Afterwards Brun had Rapperswil conquered.
The guild constitution essentially applied until 1798.

abschnitte.text: Before 1336 Zurich was ruled mainly by wealthy **merchants** and **nobles**. The craftsmen had hardly any say. In **1336** **Rudolf Brun**, with the support of the craftsmen, overthrew the old council. Many of the former councillors had to leave the city. An assembly elected Brun **for life** as the first **mayor** of Zurich.

Brun gave Zurich a new order, the **guild constitution**. The craftsmen were divided into **13 guilds**, that is, associations by trade. Their **guild masters** now sat on the council. The old noble families formed a society of their own, the **Constaffel**. In this way craftsmen and upper class shared power.

The exiled councillors wanted to return to power. In **1350** they planned a night attack on Brun and his supporters. Brun found out in time and beat the attack back. This event is called the **Zurich Night of Murder**. Because the exiles had found refuge in **Rapperswil** on Lake Zurich, Brun had the town conquered and its walls destroyed.

After this conflict Zurich feared revenge from the Habsburgs, to whom Rapperswil was close. So in **1351** Zurich made an alliance with Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden. In this way Zurich became part of the Confederation. Brun's **guild constitution** essentially remained valid until **1798**, until the end of the Old Confederation.

gewusst: The Zurich guilds still exist today: at the Sechseläuten they march through the city in old costumes.
Rudolf Brun ruled Zurich until his death in 1360.

t15e6cgm.t: Switzerland in the First World War

teile.einleitung: From 1914 to 1918 the First World War raged in Europe. Switzerland stayed neutral and did not take part in the fighting. Even so, the war years were a hard time here too.
wichtigste: The First World War lasted from 1914 to November 1918.
Switzerland stayed neutral; the General was Ulrich Wille.
Soldiers guarded the border, known as the border occupation.
A divide opened up between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland.
In 1918 over 24,000 people in Switzerland died of Spanish flu.
In November 1918 about 250,000 workers downed tools in the General Strike.

abschnitte.text: When the war began in 1914, Switzerland declared its **neutrality**. In August 1914 Parliament elected **Ulrich Wille** as General. The army was called up and guarded the borders. This period is called the **border occupation** (Grenzbesetzung). The soldiers often had to serve for a long time while their families had to cope alone at home.

Many people in **French-speaking Switzerland** felt close to France, and many German-speaking Swiss felt closer to Germany. In August 1914 Germany marched into neutral **Belgium**. This angered the French speakers in particular, because Switzerland too was neutral. The divide between the parts of the country grew deeper. On 14 December 1914 the poet **Carl Spitteler** gave the speech **“Our Swiss Standpoint”** in Zurich and called for unity.

The **International Committee of the Red Cross** in Geneva helped many people during the war. It searched for missing soldiers and looked after **prisoners of war**. In this way families could find out whether their relatives were still alive. For this work the Committee received the **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1917.

Because Switzerland had to import many foods and raw materials, these became scarce and expensive in the war. Many families had too little money for food. At the same time some firms made good money from the war. In 1918 the **Spanish flu**, a very dangerous flu, was added. Over 24,000 people in Switzerland died of it.

In November 1918, shortly after the end of the war, the **General Strike** took place. About 250,000 workers stopped work for three days. They demanded better working and living conditions. The Federal Council had troops march in, and the strike was called off. Some demands, such as shorter working hours, were nevertheless carried out in the following years.

gewusst: Carl Spitteler later received the Nobel Prize in Literature.
In the General Strike, among other things, the 48-hour week was demanded.

teile.einleitung: The Abbey Library of St Gallen is one of the oldest libraries in the world. In its splendid Baroque hall stand books that were written by hand over 1,000 years ago. Together with the abbey district it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage.
wichtigste: The Abbey Library belongs to the former monastery of St Gallen.
Many of its books were written by hand by monks over 1,000 years ago.
The monks wrote on parchment, a thin animal skin.
The splendid hall is called the Baroque Hall, and visitors wear felt slippers there.
The Egyptian mummy Shepenese lies in the library.
The abbey district has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.

abschnitte.text: The **Abbey Library** belonged to the monastery of St Gallen, which goes back to the monk **Gallus**. It is one of the oldest libraries in the world. Many of its books were written over 1,000 years ago. Among its treasures is also the famous **Plan of St Gall**. Researchers from all over the world study old manuscripts here.

In the Middle Ages there was as yet no printing. **Monks** copied the books out with quill and ink. That often took many months. They wrote on **parchment**, a thin, treated animal skin. Some books they decorated with coloured pictures and golden letters.

The great library hall is built in the **Baroque** style. It has a lot of carved wood and colourful ceiling paintings. Visitors pull big **felt slippers** over their shoes. In this way the lovely wooden floor stays protected. Above the door it says in Greek “Healing place of the soul”; people often say **“soul pharmacy”**.

A special surprise is the mummy **Shepenese**. She comes from **Egypt** and is over 2,500 years old. She lies in a painted coffin in the Baroque Hall. Since 1983 the **abbey district** with church and library has been part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**. It is therefore regarded as important for the whole of humanity.

gewusst: A real Egyptian mummy lies in the Abbey Library of St Gallen.
Books are supposed to do the soul good as medicine does the body, hence the name “soul pharmacy”.

teile.einleitung: On 22 June 1476 the Confederates defeated the army of **Charles the Bold** of Burgundy at **Murten**. After Grandson, this was the second great defeat for Charles. The battle is one of the best known in Swiss history.
wichtigste: The Battle of Murten took place on 22 June 1476.
Murten lies in the canton of Fribourg on Lake Murten.
Adrian von Bubenberg defended the besieged town.
The Burgundian army was heavily defeated.
Hans Waldmann led Zurich troops and later became mayor.
The Murten Run recalls the legend of the Murten lime tree.

abschnitte.text: After the defeat at Grandson, **Charles the Bold** gathered a new army. He marched to the little town of **Murten** on **Lake Murten** and besieged it. The Bernese **Adrian von Bubenberg** defended Murten with a small garrison. He held out until the Confederate **relief army** arrived. Relief means: help for a besieged town.

On **22 June 1476**, a good three months after Grandson, the Confederates attacked. The Burgundian army was **utterly defeated**. Many Burgundians drowned in **Lake Murten** as they fled. For Charles it was a **heavy defeat**. A year later he fell in the Battle of Nancy.

The Zurich man **Hans Waldmann** led a massed square (Gewalthaufen) at Murten. On the very day of the battle he was made a **knight**. Later he rose high in Zurich and from **1483** was **mayor** of the city. He was one of the most powerful men in the Confederation of his time.

A **legend** tells of a runner who brought the news of victory to **Fribourg**. He is said to have had a **lime twig** with him. The famous **Murten lime tree** in Fribourg is said to have grown from it. The **Murten Run**, a popular race from Murten to Fribourg, recalls this. It takes place every year in autumn.

**Murten** lies in the **canton of Fribourg** on the south-eastern shore of Lake Murten. The **town wall** is still well preserved today, and you can walk along it. The little town is bilingual: German and French are spoken here. In French it is called **Morat**.

gewusst: People say: “At Grandson Charles lost his goods, at Murten his courage.”
An obelisk near Murten commemorates the battle of 1476.

teile.einleitung: The Waldstätte, or Forest Cantons, is the name for the three states of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden in Central Switzerland. They are regarded as the founders of the Confederation and are therefore also called the founding cantons. From them Switzerland has its name, and Lake Lucerne its name too.
wichtigste: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden founded the Confederation.
Together they are also called the founding cantons.
The canton of Schwyz gave Switzerland its name.
Unterwalden is today divided into Obwalden and Nidwalden.
In the coat of arms of Uri a bull on a yellow background can be seen.
The main towns are Altdorf, Schwyz, Sarnen and Stans.
The famous Gotthard Pass leads from Uri to Ticino.

abschnitte.text: The word **Waldstätte** means roughly places by the forest. What is meant are Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden around Lake Lucerne. They are regarded as the founders of the Confederation and so are also called the **founding cantons**. The landscape is marked by mountains, forests and lakes.

At the beginning of August 1291 the three valley communities made an alliance and promised each other help. The document is called the **Federal Charter** and is on display in the Museum of the Federal Charters in Schwyz. 1 August is therefore the Swiss National Day. According to tradition the Confederates swore their alliance on the **Rütli meadow** by Lake Uri.

The coat of arms of **Uri** shows a black bull's head on a yellow ground. The flag of Schwyz is red with a small white cross in the corner. From this cross the Swiss cross later arose. In the coat of arms of Obwalden and Nidwalden a **key** can be seen.

Unterwalden is today divided into two cantons: **Obwalden** with its main town Sarnen and Nidwalden with its main town Stans. The main town of Uri is called Altdorf, and the main town of Schwyz is likewise called Schwyz. Schwyz gave the whole of Switzerland its name. In all the Waldstätte German is spoken.

Through Uri leads the **Gotthard**, one of the most important Alpine crossings in Europe. Over the Gotthard Pass one reaches Ticino. Today a road tunnel and the Gotthard Base Tunnel of the railway also lead through the mountains. Even in the Middle Ages the traffic over the Gotthard brought the people of Uri tolls and work.

Many Swiss legends are set in the Waldstätte, such as the story of **William Tell** in Altdorf. It is historically certain that in 1315 the Waldstätte defeated a Habsburg army at Morgarten. Later further states such as Lucerne, Zurich and Bern joined the alliance. So from the three Waldstätte present day Switzerland grew step by step.

begriffe.erklaerung: The three first states of the Confederation: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden.
A document of 1291 in which the Waldstätte promised each other help.
An alliance of states that swore loyalty to each other with an oath.
The community of the people who live in one valley.

gewusst: Lake Lucerne is called in German the Lake of the Four Forest Cantons because the four Waldstätte of Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Lucerne lie on it.
The Swiss cross goes back to the small white cross in the red flag of Schwyz.

teile.einleitung: The Social Democratic Party of Switzerland, SP for short, was founded in 1888. It arose from the labour movement and campaigned for better living conditions for working men and women. It is one of the oldest parties in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The SP was founded on 21 October 1888.
The first party programme was written by Albert Steck of Bern.
The first president was Alexander Reichel.
The programme of 1888 relied on democratic reforms instead of revolution.
In 1890 Jakob Vogelsanger was elected to the National Council as the first Social Democrat.
Only with proportional representation from 1919 did the SP parliamentary group grow strongly.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century many people worked in **factories**. The working days were long and the wages low. Working men and women joined together to defend themselves. In 1880 the **Swiss Trade Union Federation** was founded. It united the trade unions at national level and later worked closely with the SP.

On 21 October 1888 a Swiss Workers' Day decided to found the **Social Democratic Party of Switzerland**. Earlier social democratic parties had lasted only a short time. The first president was **Alexander Reichel** of Bern. After him **Albert Steck**, who had written the first party programme, took over the leadership.

Albert Steck's programme wanted to solve the **social question** by democratic means. By that was meant the hardship and poor conditions of the workers. The programme rejected revolution and relied on the means of **direct democracy**. In 1904 the party then gave itself a Marxist programme. Marxist means that it was based on the ideas of Karl Marx.

In 1890 the Zurich man **Jakob Vogelsanger** entered the **National Council** as the first Social Democrat. But the SP remained a small parliamentary group for a long time. The reason was the **majority voting system**: the majority in a constituency won all the seats, and minorities got nothing. From 1919 **proportional representation** applied, in which the seats are shared out according to the share of votes. After that the SP group grew strongly.

gewusst: Only in 1943 was the first Social Democrat, Ernst Nobs, elected to the Federal Council.
The change from majority voting to proportional representation in 1919 greatly changed the Swiss Parliament.

teile.einleitung: The solar wind sail was an experiment of the University of Bern. In 1969 it travelled to the Moon with Apollo 11 and caught tiny particles from the Sun there. It was the only non-American experiment on the first Moon landing.
wichtigste: The solar wind sail was planned and built at the University of Bern.
It went to the Moon with Apollo 11 in July 1969.
Buzz Aldrin set it up even before the US flag.
The sail was made of thin aluminium foil, and the device weighed about 430 grams.
It caught tiny particles of the solar wind.
The foil was brought back to Earth and examined in Bern.

abschnitte.text: From the Sun tiny particles fly constantly out into space. This stream is called the **solar wind**. On Earth the particles hardly arrive, because the magnetic field and the air hold them back. On the Moon there is no air. So the solar wind can be caught there directly.

Researchers at the **Physics Institute** of the **University of Bern** planned the experiment. They wanted to find out what the solar wind is made of. For this they built a sail from thin **aluminium foil**. The whole device weighed only about 430 grams. It was the only non-American experiment on the first Moon landing.

In July 1969 **Apollo 11** landed on the Moon. For the first time humans set foot on the Moon. **Buzz Aldrin**, the second person on the Moon, pushed the sail into the lunar soil. It was even set up before the American flag. In this way it could collect particles for as long as possible.

The particles stayed stuck in the foil. The astronauts took the foil back to Earth with them. In **Bern** the particles were measured exactly in the laboratory. The sail afterwards flew on further **Apollo** Moon flights. The measurements helped to learn more about the Sun.

gewusst: The Bernese solar wind sail stood in front of the US flag on the Moon.
A small Swiss experiment was part of the most famous Moon landing.

teile.einleitung: The **Habsburg** is a castle in the canton of Aargau, not far from Brugg. It is the **ancestral castle** of the Habsburgs, a family that later supplied kings and emperors in Europe. Today you can visit the castle.
wichtigste: The Habsburg stands on the Wülpelsberg, a wooded hill.
It lies a few kilometres from Brugg.
It is the ancestral castle of the Habsburg family.
The name is often explained as “hawk's castle”, but this is not certain.
The old coat of arms showed a red lion on a yellow ground.
The Habsburgs later became kings and emperors.
Today there is a restaurant and an exhibition in the castle.

abschnitte.text: The Habsburg stands on the **Wülpelsberg**, a **wooded hill** in the **canton of Aargau**. It lies only a few kilometres from **Brugg**. It was built in the 11th century. An **ancestral castle** is the castle after which a family is named. So the Habsburg is the ancestral castle of the **Habsburgs**.

One well-known explanation says the name comes from **“Habichtsburg”**, that is, a hawk's castle. Other researchers think of an old word for bank or crossing. **None** of the explanations is certain. The old **coat of arms** of the Counts of Habsburg showed a **red lion** on a yellow ground.

The Habsburgs were at first **counts** in Aargau. In 1273 **Rudolf of Habsburg** was elected king. After that the family grew more and more powerful. Many Habsburgs became **kings and emperors** and ruled over large parts of Europe, especially Austria. But they lost their old ancestral castle in Aargau: in 1415 **Bern** conquered the area.

Near **Windisch**, very close by, the Habsburg king **Albert I** was killed in 1308. At this spot his family founded **Königsfelden Abbey** from **1309**. The coloured medieval **stained-glass windows** there are still famous today. The Habsburg Agnes of Hungary lived in this abbey for a long time.

Today the Habsburg belongs to the **canton of Aargau**. In the castle there is a **restaurant** and a small **exhibition** about the castle and the family. From the tower there is a fine view over the Aare valley. Many school classes visit the castle on an outing.

gewusst: The Habsburg family still ruled Austria-Hungary until 1918, more than 600 years after the building of their little castle in Aargau.
Only part of the original castle still stands today; another part is preserved only as a ruin.

teile.einleitung: In the 15th and 16th centuries foreign princes paid money to the Confederate states and to influential men. These payments were called **pensions**. They secured the princes mercenaries and political friendship, but were very controversial.
wichtigste: Pensions were payments from foreign princes to states and to individuals.
Public pensions went to the states, private pensions to individual people.
In 1503 the Federal Diet wanted to ban private pensions with the Pensions Charter.
The people mockingly called bribable gentlemen “crown-eaters” (Kronenfresser).
In 1513 the Bernese country people rose up in the Köniz Uprising.
Zwingli fought against pensions and mercenary service.

abschnitte.text: Foreign rulers, above all the King of **France**, needed Swiss **mercenaries**. To be allowed to recruit them, they paid money. If the money went to a state's treasury, it was called a **public pension**. If it went to individual powerful men, it was a **private pension**. These private payments in particular were seen by many as **bribery**.

Many pensions were paid in **crowns**, a French gold coin. So the people mockingly called politicians who let themselves be paid by foreign princes **“Kronenfresser”** (crown-eaters). The name shows how great the anger was at the bribable gentlemen. In 1503 the Federal Diet tried to ban private money and unauthorised mercenary service with the **Pensions Charter**. But the decision could not be enforced and was soon repealed.

After the Dijon Expedition of 1513 farmers from the Köniz area marched to Bern. They demanded that the pension gentlemen be punished. This uprising is called the **Köniz Uprising**. Similar unrest also occurred in **Lucerne** and **Solothurn**. The country people felt that a few were getting rich while their sons died in foreign wars.

The Zurich reformer **Ulrich Zwingli** was a sharp opponent of pensions. In 1521 the Confederate states made a mercenary alliance with France. **Zurich** was the only state that did not join. In 1522 Zurich banned pensions and mercenary service entirely. In the same year Zwingli warned against foreign military service in his work **“Divine Admonition to the Confederates at Schwyz”**.

Families that received pensions and led mercenary regiments became rich and politically influential. In this way money and offices were concentrated in the hands of a few families. In the long term this encouraged the rise of the **patriciate** in the cities and of leading **magistrate families** in the countryside.

gewusst: The word “pension” at that time did not mean a retirement pension but a regular payment of money.
Zwingli himself took part in campaigns in Italy as a field preacher and knew the mercenary system from his own experience.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages the area of present-day Switzerland belonged to the Holy Roman Empire. An area was **imperially free** (reichsfrei) if it had no count or duke over it but was directly subject to the king or emperor. For the forest cantons this was very important.
wichtigste: Imperially free meant: directly subject to the king or emperor.
In 1231 Uri was the first of the forest cantons to receive a charter of freedom.
It was issued by King Henry (VII), the son of Emperor Frederick II.
This freed Uri from the rule of the Habsburgs.
Schwyz received its charter of freedom at Faenza in Italy.
In 1309 Henry VII also confirmed imperial freedom for Unterwalden.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages most areas had a **count** or **duke** as their lord. He stood between the people and the king. **Imperially free** areas, by contrast, were subject **directly to the king** or emperor. But the king was far away. So people could arrange many things themselves. A representative of the king was called an **imperial bailiff** (Reichsvogt).

Uri lay on the way to the **Gotthard**. This pass was very important for the Empire and for trade with Italy. Uri had previously been pledged to the counts of **Habsburg**. In **1231** King **Henry (VII)** bought the valley back and issued a **charter of freedom**. He promised never to give Uri away again. Henry (VII) was the son of Emperor Frederick II.

Warriors from Schwyz helped Emperor **Frederick II** in the siege of the city of **Faenza** in Italy. As thanks, the emperor issued them a **charter of freedom** there in 1240. The Habsburgs, however, did not recognise this charter. Later they tried again and again to assert their rights in Schwyz.

In **1309** King **Henry VII** of the House of Luxembourg issued charters of freedom for all three **forest cantons**. With this, **Unterwalden** too was now imperially free. Imperial freedom was an important basis for Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden later being able to hold their own against the Habsburgs. Cities such as Bern and Zurich were also imperially free.

gewusst: Uri's charter of freedom from 1231 is still kept today in the State Archive in Altdorf.
King Henry (VII) is written with brackets because in the later numbering of the kings another ruler received the number VII.

teile.einleitung: The White Book of Sarnen is a manuscript from around 1470. It contains the oldest known account of the liberation of the Waldstätte, with Tell and the Rütli. For research it is an important but late source.
wichtigste: The author was the Obwalden land clerk Hans Schriber.
The book was written between 1470 and 1472.
It has its name from the white binding of the 17th century.
Here the Rütli is mentioned for the first time as a meeting place.
Gerold Meyer von Knonau made the book known to research in 1854.
Joseph Eutych Kopp showed in 1835 that the bailiffs cannot be proved in documents.

abschnitte.titel: A book with a white cover
abschnitte.text: The **White Book of Sarnen** was written between **1470 and 1472**. Its author was the Obwalden land clerk **Hans Schriber**. A land clerk was a clerk in the service of the state. The book contains copies of **alliances** and a **chronicle** about the liberation. It has its name from the **white binding** of pigskin. This dates only from the 17th century and has nothing to do with the contents.

The chronicle tells of wicked **bailiffs** who oppressed the people. The bailiff **Landenberg** has the **oxen** of a farmer in the **Melchtal** taken away. So the young man of the **Melchtal** joins the conspirators. He meets **Stauffacher** and **Fürst** at night on the **Rütli**. This place is mentioned here for the first time. William Tell also appears in the chronicle. The **castle of Sarnen** is taken by a ruse: subjects bring the bailiff gifts and leave the gate open, and at a horn signal the allies storm in.

The book arose about 180 years after the **Federal Charter** of 1291. So it is not a **contemporary source**. In **1835** the historian **Joseph Eutych Kopp** compared the chronicles with old documents. He found no evidence for the bailiffs **Gessler** and Landenberg. With that the critical examination of the story of the liberation began. In 1854 the Zurich state archivist **Gerold Meyer von Knonau** came upon the book in Sarnen and published the text in 1857.

abschnitte.titel: An apple shot in the north
abschnitte.text: A similar story also exists in the north of Europe. Around 1200 **Saxo Grammaticus** tells of the archer **Toko**. He had to shoot an apple from his son's head. Many researchers see in this **Toko legend** a possible model for the Tell story. Whether Tell really existed is therefore disputed.

gewusst: In Sarnen itself the White Book was always known; only the rest of research did not know it for a long time.
Friedrich Schiller's drama “William Tell” of 1804 takes up many scenes that are already in the White Book.

teile.einleitung: In the 1980s “forest dieback” (Waldsterben) caused great worry in Switzerland. Many trees showed damaged crowns, and air pollution was held to be the cause. The debate led to important environmental laws.
wichtigste: Forest dieback shaped the environmental debate above all in the 1980s.
Air pollution and acid rain were held to be the main cause.
In 1985 the Federal Council issued the Ordinance on Air Pollution Control.
From 1987 the catalytic converter became in effect compulsory for new petrol cars.
Since 1985 the Sanasilva programme has recorded the state of the forests.
The feared large scale destruction of the forests did not occur.

abschnitte.text: At the start of the **1980s** surveys showed many trees with damaged **tree crowns**. Needles and leaves became thinner or changed colour. Many people feared that the forests might soon disappear. **Forest dieback** became a major political issue. In Switzerland this is especially important, because many forests protect villages and roads from **avalanches** and rockfall.

The main cause was held to be **air pollution**. Traffic, industry and heating gave off **sulphur dioxide** and **nitrogen oxides**. These substances combine with water in the air. In this way **acid rain** arises. It can damage leaves and soils. Many therefore demanded that the air be made cleaner quickly.

Politics reacted. In 1983 the **Environmental Protection Act** came into being. In 1985 the Federal Council issued the **Ordinance on Air Pollution Control**, **LRV** for short. It set limit values for pollutants and came into force in 1986. From **1987** the **catalytic converter** became in effect compulsory for new petrol cars. It greatly reduces the output of nitrogen oxides. In the same decade, on 1 November 1986, a warehouse of Sandoz burned at **Schweizerhalle**. With the firefighting water poisons got into the Rhine, which turned red, and many fish died.

Since 1985 the **Sanasilva** programme has regularly recorded the state of the tree crowns. Today research mostly says: the feared large scale destruction of the forests **did not occur**. The measures against air pollution contributed to this. In addition some forecasts were too pessimistic. Many experts stress, however, that the warnings set important **environmental laws** in motion.

gewusst: The name “Sanasilva” comes from Latin and means roughly “healthy forest”.
About a third of the area of Switzerland is covered with forest.

teile.einleitung: The **Pontifical Swiss Guard** protects the Pope in the Vatican in Rome. It consists only of Swiss men and was founded as long ago as 1506. With its colourful uniform it is world-famous.
wichtigste: The Swiss Guard was founded in 1506 by Pope Julius II.
It works in the Vatican, the Pope's small state in Rome.
A member of the Guard is called a guardsman.
Guardsmen must be Swiss citizens and Catholic.
The full-dress uniform is striped in blue, yellow and red.
New guardsmen are sworn in every year on 6 May.

abschnitte.text: Pope **Julius II** wanted reliable soldiers to protect him. Swiss mercenaries had a very good reputation at the time. On **22 January 1506** about 150 Swiss men marched into Rome. This day is seen as the **founding day** of the Guard. This makes it one of the oldest troops in the world that still exist today.

On **6 May 1527** foreign troops attacked Rome. This sack is called the **Sacco di Roma**. Many guardsmen died protecting the Pope. The Pope was able to get to safety. In memory of this, new guardsmen are sworn in every year on **6 May**.

A member is called a **guardsman**. He must be a **Swiss citizen** and **Catholic**. He must also be a young man who has completed recruit school in the Swiss army. The guardsmen commit themselves for at least two years. At the oath they raise three fingers of the right hand.

The famous **full-dress uniform** is striped in **blue, yellow and red**. On ceremonial occasions the guardsmen wear a helmet and carry a **halberd**. This is a long pole weapon with an axe blade and a spike. In everyday duty they wear a simpler blue uniform. For their security tasks they now also use modern equipment.

gewusst: The Swiss Guard is regarded as the smallest army in the world.
It is the only permitted exception to the ban on Swiss citizens serving in foreign armies.

teile.einleitung: Swiss television began in 1953 with trial broadcasts from a small studio in Zurich. At first there was only one hour of programmes in the evening, and the picture was black and white. Today television is hard to imagine away from everyday life.
wichtigste: In July 1953 the trial service of Swiss television started in Zurich.
The first studio was called Studio Bellerive and was in the Seefeld district.
At first there was about one hour of programmes on five evenings a week.
The Tagesschau news already existed in the trial period.
Since 1 February 1965 there has been advertising on Swiss television.
On 1 October 1968 colour television began.

abschnitte.text: In July 1953 Swiss television started its **trial service**. Broadcasts came from **Studio Bellerive** in the Seefeld district of Zurich. There was about one hour of programmes on five evenings a week. After that the screen was empty again. Television was run by the **SRG**, which already operated radio.

At first hardly anyone owned a television, because the sets were expensive. Only about 920 people had a **television licence**, that is, a permit to watch television. Most of them were **innkeepers**. The guests watched together in the restaurants. Only gradually did families buy their own sets too.

The **Tagesschau** already existed in the trial period. It is the oldest news programme on Swiss television. It still runs every evening today. The first pictures were **black and white**; the sets showed only shades of grey.

On 1 February 1965 the first **advertising** ran on Swiss television. At first it was limited to a few minutes a day. With the money from advertising, television could make more programmes. In addition, households still pay a fee for radio and television today.

On 1 October 1968 **colour television** began in Switzerland. A colour television cost about 3,000 francs at the time, a great deal of money. So for years many people still watched in black and white. Today there are programmes in all the national languages, in German, French, Italian and partly Romansh.

gewusst: The Tagesschau has been broadcast since the trial period of 1953 and is therefore older than colour television.
In the past, anyone who wanted to watch television needed an official licence.

teile.einleitung: Rodolphe Lindt was a chocolate maker from Bern. In 1879 he invented **conching**, a process that makes chocolate smooth and melting. His invention changed chocolate all over the world.
wichtigste: Rodolphe Lindt had his factory in the Matte district of Bern.
In 1879 he invented conching.
A conche stirs the warm chocolate mass for many hours.
The name comes from the Spanish word “concha” for shell.
The new chocolate was called melting chocolate.
In 1899 Johann Rudolf Sprüngli bought the firm, and so Lindt & Sprüngli was created.

abschnitte.text: In **1879** Rodolphe Lindt opened a small chocolate factory in the **Matte**, a district on the River Aare in **Bern**. At that time chocolate was usually hard, grainy and slightly bitter. It did not melt nicely in the mouth. Lindt wanted to change that and tried out a great deal.

Lindt built a machine that **stirs and rubs** the warm chocolate mass **for many hours**. This process is called **conching**. The machine is called a **conche** because its trough looked like a **shell**. In Spanish a shell is called **“concha”**. The long stirring makes the mass very fine, and unpleasant flavours disappear.

The new chocolate was **smooth** and **melted on the tongue**. So it was called **melting chocolate**. It quickly became very popular. Lindt's invention contributed a great deal to Switzerland becoming famous for its fine chocolate. To this day almost all makers conche their chocolate.

In **1899** the Zurich chocolate maker **Johann Rudolf Sprüngli** bought Lindt's factory together with the secret of conching. This created the firm **Lindt & Sprüngli**. Its headquarters is now in **Kilchberg** on Lake Zurich. The Lindt brand is known all over the world.

gewusst: The story goes that Lindt owed his invention to chance: a machine kept running over the weekend, and the mass was especially fine afterwards.
Sprüngli is said to have paid 1.5 million gold francs for the factory and the secret of conching.

teile.einleitung: After the fall of Napoleon, Europe was reorganised at the Congress of Vienna. In 1815 the Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva joined the Confederation as new cantons. Switzerland now had 22 cantons.
wichtigste: In 1815 the Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva joined the Confederation.
This gave Switzerland 22 cantons.
From 1810 to 1813 the Valais was the French département of Simplon.
Neuchâtel was at once a canton and a principality of the King of Prussia.
Geneva received municipalities such as Carouge and Versoix.
In return Bern received the former Prince-Bishopric of Basel in the Jura.

abschnitte.text: After the fall of **Napoleon** the great powers met at the **Congress of Vienna**. They redrew the borders in Europe. Switzerland too was given a new shape. In 1815 the **Valais**, **Neuchâtel** and **Geneva** joined as new cantons. Since then Switzerland has had roughly its present borders.

**Napoleon** wanted to control the important **Simplon road** over the Alps. So in 1810 he made the Valais the French **département of Simplon**. After his fall the Valais became free. In 1815 it joined the Confederation. Its capital is **Sion** (German: Sitten), which had long been a bishop's seat.

**Neuchâtel** had a special position. It was a Swiss canton and at the same time a **principality** of the **King of Prussia**. On 1 March **1848** republicans in Neuchâtel proclaimed the **republic**. Prussia, however, did not recognise this at once. Only in **1857** did the Prussian king finally give up Neuchâtel.

**Geneva** had been annexed by **France** in 1798. It became the capital of the **département of Léman**. In 1815 Geneva joined the Confederation. But the Geneva territory was surrounded by foreign land. So it was given municipalities from **Savoy** and France, for example **Carouge** and **Versoix**. This created a link with the rest of Switzerland.

Bern had earlier ruled **Vaud** and **Aargau**. These areas had meanwhile become cantons in their own right. In compensation Bern received in 1815 most of the former **Prince-Bishopric of Basel** in the Jura. Many people there were not happy with this. Much later part of this area became the **canton of Jura**.

gewusst: Until 1848 one Swiss canton had a king as its prince: Neuchâtel.
At the Congress of Vienna in 1815 Switzerland's neutrality was also recognised.

teile.einleitung: Dormant assets are bank deposits whose owners have not been in touch for a long time. In the 1990s there was a major debate about them. It was about accounts of Holocaust victims in Swiss banks.
wichtigste: Dormant assets are accounts with no contact with the owner.
In the 1990s the debate was mainly about accounts of Holocaust victims.
The World Jewish Congress pushed the debate strongly forward.
From 1996 the Volcker Commission had millions of accounts checked.
In 1997 the security guard Christoph Meili saved documents from destruction.
In 1998 UBS and Credit Suisse reached a settlement for 1.25 billion dollars.

abschnitte.text: A bank account is **dormant** when the bank no longer has contact with the owner. Perhaps he has died, and his heirs know nothing about the account. In the **Second World War** many persecuted people brought their money to Switzerland. Many of them were murdered in the **Holocaust**. Their families were often later unable to get the money back because proof was missing.

In the **1990s** the subject became known worldwide. The **World Jewish Congress** under Edgar Bronfman demanded clarification and the return of the money. It was supported by the US senator **Alfonse D'Amato**. In the USA those affected filed **class actions** against Swiss banks. In a class action many people sue together.

There was heated discussion in Switzerland. At the end of 1996 the President of the Confederation, **Jean-Pascal Delamuraz**, spoke of “blackmail” in connection with the demands. This caused outrage, and he later apologised. The Swiss ambassador in the USA, **Carlo Jagmetti**, had written of a “war” in an internal report. When the paper became public he resigned in January 1997.

In January 1997 **Christoph Meili** was working as a security guard at the Swiss Bank Corporation. In the shredding room he found old documents from the time of the Second World War. They were due to be destroyed. Meili took them with him and handed them to a **Jewish organisation**. The case caused a great stir internationally.

From **1996** the **Volcker Commission**, led by the former US central bank chief **Paul Volcker**, searched the Swiss banks. It had millions of accounts checked and found about **54,000** accounts with a possible link to Holocaust victims. In August **1998** the big banks **UBS** and **Credit Suisse** reached an agreement with the plaintiffs. They paid **1.25 billion dollars**, and the class actions were settled.

gewusst: The Volcker Commission's checking of the accounts lasted several years.
The federal government also had Switzerland's role in the Second World War examined by an independent commission of historians, the Bergier Commission.

teile.einleitung: In 1803 six new cantons were created in Switzerland. At that time Napoleon gave Switzerland a new order with the Act of Mediation. Former subject territories and allies became cantons with equal rights.
wichtigste: In 1803 the Act of Mediation created six new cantons.
The new cantons were St Gallen, the Grisons, Aargau, Thurgau, Ticino and Vaud.
The Fricktal had previously belonged to Austria and went to Aargau.
Karl Müller-Friedberg is seen as the founder of the canton of St Gallen.
Before 1798 Thurgau was a common lordship.
In Ticino the capital alternated between three towns until 1878.
The coat of arms of Vaud bears the words “Liberté et Patrie”.

abschnitte.text: After the French invaded in 1798 there was a great deal of conflict in Switzerland. So in **1803** **Napoleon** gave Switzerland a new constitution, the **Act of Mediation**. Mediation means acting as a go-between. Switzerland now consisted of **19 cantons**. Six of them were new: **St Gallen, the Grisons, Aargau, Thurgau, Ticino and Vaud**.

The canton of **Aargau** was put together from several areas. They included the **Bernese Aargau**, the **County of Baden** and the **Free Bailiwicks**. The **Fricktal** was added too. It had long been **Habsburg-Austrian**. Aarau became the capital.

The new canton of **St Gallen** was formed from very different regions. From 1803 it was led for almost thirty years by **Karl Müller-Friedberg**. He is seen as the founding father of the canton. Before 1798 **Thurgau** was a **common lordship**, that is, a subject territory of several Confederate states. Its capital became **Frauenfeld**, where the bailiff had sat earlier too.

**Ticino** too had earlier been a subject territory of the Confederates. The young canton had no fixed capital. **Bellinzona, Lugano and Locarno** took turns. Only in **1878** did Bellinzona become the permanent capital. **Vaud** had belonged to Bern until 1798. Its motto **“Liberté et Patrie”** means “Freedom and Fatherland”.

The **Grisons** had previously been an **associate state** (Zugewandter Ort), that is, an ally of the Confederates. It consisted of the **Three Leagues**: the Grey League, the League of God's House and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions. In 1803 it became a full canton. To this day the Grisons is the largest canton of Switzerland by area.

gewusst: From 1798 there were no more subject territories; in 1803 several former subject territories became cantons with equal rights.
Ticino had three capitals in turn until 1878.

teile.einleitung: On 1 August Switzerland celebrates its national holiday. It recalls the founding of the Confederation. All over the country there are fires, lanterns, speeches and festivities.
wichtigste: The Swiss National Day is on 1 August.
It recalls the Federal Charter of 1291.
In the evening large bonfires burn on hills and mountains.
Children walk through the village with glowing lanterns.
The 1 August bread roll (1.-August-Weggli) with a cross cut into it is part of the holiday.
The President of the Confederation gives an address.

abschnitte.text: The holiday recalls the **Federal Charter** of 1291. In it Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden promised each other mutual help. The charter is dated to the beginning of August 1291. The date is therefore seen as the birthday of the Confederation. 1 August has only been celebrated since 1891, for the 600th anniversary. Since 1994 it has been a **public holiday** throughout Switzerland.

In the evening large **bonfires** burn on many hills and mountains. They can be seen from far away. In the past such fires on mountains also served as warning signals. In many places there is also a **firework display**. Children light volcanoes and sparklers.

Many children go for a walk in the evening with **lanterns**. The lanterns often show a Swiss cross or a cantonal coat of arms. Houses and streets are decorated with flags. In many municipalities there is a festival with music, food and a speech.

Around the national holiday bakeries sell the **1 August bread roll** (1.-August-Weggli). It has a cross cut into it. Often a little Swiss flag is stuck in it. Many families have breakfast together on 1 August, some on a farm at a **Buurezmorge** (farmers' breakfast).

The **President of the Confederation** gives an address to the whole population on 1 August. It is shown on radio and television. In the municipalities too, politicians give speeches. A special celebration takes place every year on the **Rütli meadow** on Lake Lucerne.

gewusst: In 1993 1 August was made a nationwide holiday by a popular vote.
The Federal Charter of 1291 is now kept in the Museum of the Federal Charters in Schwyz.

teile.einleitung: Through Switzerland runs a language border between German-speaking Switzerland and French-speaking Romandy. It arose over many centuries. Sometimes it also shows itself in votes.
wichtigste: The language border separates German-speaking Switzerland from Romandy.
The symbol of the border is the Saane, in French the Sarine.
Jokingly the border is called the Röstigraben.
Bern, Fribourg and Valais are officially bilingual in German and French.
Biel/Bienne is an officially bilingual city.
In Valais the border runs roughly between Sierre and Leuk.

abschnitte.text: The language border arose slowly over several centuries. In the **early Middle Ages** the **Alemanni** settled in the area of present-day German-speaking Switzerland and brought their language with them. In the west people went on speaking a **Romance** language, from which French developed. So the border gradually took shape. It follows no cantonal border and no straight line.

The symbol of the border is the **Saane**, in French the **Sarine**. It flows through the canton of Fribourg. Jokingly people speak of the **Röstigraben** (“rösti ditch”). The expression alludes to **rösti**, which is regarded as typically German-Swiss. It is often used when the two parts of the country decide differently in a vote.

Three cantons are officially bilingual in German and French: **Bern**, **Fribourg** and **Valais**. In Valais the border runs roughly between **Sierre** and **Leuk**. Between them lies the **Pfynwald**. **The Grisons** is even trilingual, with German, Romansh and Italian.

In **Biel/Bienne** street signs, authorities and schools are bilingual. Many people there switch between the two languages in daily life. The small town of **Murten** (Morat) in the canton of Fribourg also lies close to the language border. There the majority speak German. On the border many children learn both languages early.

gewusst: Biel/Bienne officially bears its name in both languages.
Rösti has become the namesake of a language border.

teile.einleitung: Marie Heim-Vögtlin was the first Swiss woman doctor. In her time almost only men were allowed to study medicine. With courage and perseverance she opened the way into this profession for women.
wichtigste: Marie Heim-Vögtlin was the first woman doctor in Switzerland.
She was born in 1845 in Bözen in the canton of Aargau.
From 1868 she studied medicine at the University of Zurich.
In 1874 she completed her studies as a doctor of medicine.
She treated mainly women and children.
Her husband Albert Heim was a well-known geologist.
In 1901 she founded a nursing school with a hospital together with other women.

abschnitte.text: Marie Vögtlin was born in **1845** in **Bözen** in the canton of **Aargau**. Her father was the **pastor** there. In those days girls were mainly supposed to learn how to run a household. Studying was almost impossible for women. But Marie wanted to learn more and help sick people.

Anyone who wants to become a doctor has to study **medicine**. Marie Vögtlin began her studies at the **University of Zurich** in **1868**. Zurich admitted women as students quite early. Many people thought this was improper at the time. Marie did not let herself be discouraged. She was the first Swiss woman to study medicine there.

In **1874** she became a **doctor of medicine**. Afterwards she opened her own **practice** in Zurich. That was something completely new at the time. In her practice she helped mainly **women and children**. Many patients were glad to be treated by a woman.

Marie Vögtlin married **Albert Heim**. He studied mountains and rocks and was a well-known **geologist** in Zurich. From then on she was called **Marie Heim-Vögtlin**. She carried on working as a doctor after her marriage. That was very unusual for a woman at the time.

In **1901** she helped to found the **Swiss Nursing School** with a hospital in Zurich. There women learned the profession of **nursing**. In the hospital, women doctors and nurses worked together. Marie Heim-Vögtlin died in 1916. To this day she is seen as a role model for women in medicine.

gewusst: The University of Zurich was one of the first in Europe to admit women to study.
At the time of her studies there were only very few women students at the University of Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Rationing means that scarce goods are shared out to everyone in fixed amounts. During the Second World War from 1939 to 1945, and for some years afterwards, people in Switzerland could get food only in exchange for coupons on a ration card. This was so that nobody would go hungry, even though the country was getting almost no goods from abroad.
wichtigste: Rationing means that each person may buy only a fixed amount of a scarce product.
On 29 August 1939 the federal government imposed a purchase ban on important foods such as sugar, fats and cereal products.
From 30 October 1939 basic foods such as sugar, pulses and fats were formally rationed.
Switzerland was better prepared than in the First World War because the war economy machinery had been ready for use since 1938.
Bread was only rationed from October 1942.
With the Anbauschlacht, also called the Wahlen Plan, the area of arable land was almost doubled.
Only in July 1948 were the last foods released from rationing.

abschnitte.text: In **rationing** the state shares out scarce goods fairly. Each person receives a **ration card** with small coupons. In the shop you had to hand over the right coupon as well as the money. Anyone who had no coupons left could not buy that product again until the next month.

Right at the start of the war, on 29 August 1939, the federal government imposed a **purchase ban** on sugar, fats and cereal products. This meant people could no longer stock up on huge supplies. From 30 October 1939 sugar, pulses and fats were formally rationed. Because the **war economy** had been prepared since 1938, supply worked better than in the First World War.

In the course of the war more and more goods were added, such as meat, cheese, milk, clothes, soap and petrol. From May 1941 there were two **meatless days** per week. From October 1942 even bread was rationed. Wartime nutrition planning allowed about 2,160 calories per day for an adult.

There were different cards for different needs. **Card B** offered more coupons for bread, milk and cheese instead of meat. For children and for people doing heavy work there were adjusted amounts. Many families also saved extra and kept hens or rabbits.

So that Switzerland could grow more of its own food, the agronomist **Friedrich Traugott Wahlen** developed a plan. He presented it publicly on 15 November 1940 in a lecture in Zurich. The programme is called the **Anbauschlacht** (“battle for crops”) or the Wahlen Plan. The area of open arable land grew from about 183,000 hectares in 1940 to about 352,000 hectares in 1945.

Thanks to the Anbauschlacht, the **degree of self-sufficiency** in food rose from about 52 to about 70 per cent. Even so, Switzerland could not manage entirely without imports. After the war ended in 1945, rationing was relaxed only step by step. In July 1948 the last foods were released from rationing.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small section of the card that you had to hand over when shopping, in addition to money.
A ban on buying a product for a time so that nobody hoards it.
The share of food that a country produces itself.
Planning of food, raw materials and labour by the state in wartime.
A programme in the Second World War to create far more fields in Switzerland.

gewusst: During the Anbauschlacht even parks and sports grounds in cities were dug up; in Zurich, for example, potatoes grew on the Sechseläutenwiese.
Friedrich Traugott Wahlen later became a Federal Councillor and was a member of the national government from 1959 to 1965.
Rationing lasted longer in Switzerland than the war itself, namely until 1948.

teile.einleitung: The Unspunnen Festival is a big festival of Swiss folk culture in Interlaken. It is famous for the stone throwing with the Unspunnen Stone. It takes place only rarely, today about every twelve years.
wichtigste: The Unspunnen Festival takes place in Interlaken in the Bernese Oberland.
It is named after the castle ruin of Unspunnen.
The first festival took place in 1805.
In stone throwing a heavy stone is thrown as far as possible.
The Unspunnen Stone originally weighed 83.5 kilograms.
Many participants wear traditional costumes.
The stone was stolen in 1984 and in 2005.

abschnitte.titel: A festival for town and country
abschnitte.text: The **Unspunnen Festival** takes place in **Interlaken** in the Bernese Oberland. It takes its name from the nearby **castle ruin of Unspunnen**. The first festival took place in **1805**. At that time there was tension between the city of Bern and the country people. The festival was meant to bring town and country closer together again. It was celebrated a second time as early as 1808.

The best known contest is the **stone throwing**. Strong men throw the **Unspunnen Stone** as far as possible. The stone originally weighed **83.5 kilograms**. You take it on your shoulder, run up briefly and throw it away from you. Besides that at the festival there is also **Schwingen**, the Swiss wrestling, as well as yodelling and alphorn blowing.

At the Unspunnen Festival **costume groups** from all over Switzerland show their beautiful **traditional costumes**. These are traditional clothes that look different depending on the region. There are parades, dances and lots of folk music. The festival is therefore also a great costume festival. It does not take place every year but today roughly **every twelve years**. It was last celebrated in 2017.

The Unspunnen Stone has an adventurous history. In **1984** it was stolen, by Jura separatists. They were fighting at that time for the independence of the Jura from the canton of Bern. Only in **2001** did the stone come back. In **2005** it was stolen again and has been missing ever since. That is why a **copy** is thrown today.

gewusst: The real Unspunnen Stone has still not turned up again.
Between 1808 and 1905 no Unspunnen Festival took place for almost a hundred years.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Psalm is the national anthem of Switzerland. It begins with the words “Trittst im Morgenrot daher” (“When you step forth in the red of dawn”). It is heard on 1 August and before international matches of the Swiss national team.
wichtigste: The national anthem of Switzerland is called the Swiss Psalm.
The melody was written in 1841 by the monk Alberik Zwyssig from Wettingen Abbey.
The words were written by the Zurich man Leonhard Widmer.
In 1961 the Swiss Psalm was declared the anthem provisionally; since 1981 it has been so for good.
Before that people sang “Rufst du, mein Vaterland” to the melody of the British royal anthem.

abschnitte.text: The melody comes from **Alberik Zwyssig**, a monk from **Wettingen Abbey**. He wrote it in 1841. The words were written by the Zurich man **Leonhard Widmer**. Together they became the **Swiss Psalm**. A psalm is a solemn song that praises God.

The German text begins with the words **“Trittst im Morgenrot daher”**. The anthem describes sun, mountains and nature. Each verse mentions a different time of day or a different kind of weather. Again and again God is spoken of, watching over the land. The text exists in German, French, Italian and Romansh.

In the past Switzerland sang **“Rufst du, mein Vaterland”**. This song had the same melody as the **British royal anthem**. At state visits and sporting events that led to mix-ups. So people looked for an anthem of their own. In 1961 the Federal Council first declared the Swiss Psalm the national anthem provisionally.

Since **1981** the Swiss Psalm has been the official **national anthem** for good. It is sung, for example, on **1 August**. It is played before international matches of the Swiss national team, and at medal ceremonies too. Many people, however, know only the first verse by heart.

gewusst: The melody of the Swiss national anthem was composed by a monk.
The old Swiss anthem sounded exactly the same as the anthem of Great Britain.

teile.einleitung: From 1934 to 2002 the **seasonal workers' statute** (Saisonnierstatut) regulated how foreign workers were allowed to work in Switzerland for some months of the year. These people were called **seasonal workers** (Saisonniers). They did a great deal to build up Switzerland, but had only a few rights.
wichtigste: Seasonal workers were only allowed to work in Switzerland for one season.
They worked especially in construction, hospitality and agriculture.
In the 1950s and 1960s most of them came from Italy.
They received the permit A.
Bringing their families was in principle forbidden to them.
Max Frisch wrote: “We called for workers, and human beings came.”

abschnitte.text: The basis was the **Federal Act on the Residence and Settlement of Foreigners**, **ANAG** for short, of 1931. The Federal Council brought the seasonal workers' statute into force in **1934**. Seasonal workers received a permit for one **season**. After that they had to leave Switzerland again. Their permit bore the letter **A**. Annual residents had permit B, settled residents permit C.

Seasonal workers worked mainly in **construction**, **hospitality** and **agriculture**. These sectors need many workers depending on the time of year. After the Second World War the economy grew strongly. In 1948 Switzerland made a recruitment agreement with **Italy**. Later many people also came from **Spain**, **Portugal** and **Yugoslavia**.

Many Italian seasonal workers had to undergo a medical examination at the border stations in **Brig** and **Chiasso**. Anyone judged to be ill was sent back. The workers often lived in simple huts. Their life in Switzerland was marked by hard work and insecurity.

Seasonal workers were in principle not allowed to bring their **families** to Switzerland. Only after several full seasons was this possible, under strict conditions. Even so, many parents secretly brought their children with them. Thousands of children lived **hidden** in flats. They were not allowed to attract attention and often could neither play outside nor go to school.

The writer **Max Frisch** wrote the famous sentence in 1965: **“We called for workers, and human beings came.”** With this he criticised the fact that people were seen only as workers. In 1981 the **Mitenand initiative** demanded a more supportive policy on foreigners and the end of the statute. It was rejected with over 80 per cent against. Only with the **free movement of persons** with the EU was the statute abolished in 2002.

gewusst: Many of Switzerland's roads, tunnels and dams were built largely by seasonal workers.
The story of the hidden children only became widely known in recent decades.

teile.einleitung: The Plan of St Gall is a drawing from the early Middle Ages. It shows what an ideal monastery should look like. It is the oldest surviving drawn plan of a monastery and about 1,200 years old.
wichtigste: The monastery plan was made around 825 in the Carolingian period.
It was drawn at Reichenau Abbey in Lake Constance and sent to St Gallen.
It consists of five pieces of parchment sewn together.
It shows a whole monastery with a church, stables, gardens and workshops.
The monastery of St Gallen was not built exactly according to the plan.
The plan is today in the Abbey Library of St Gallen.

abschnitte.text: The **Plan of St Gall** was made around the year 825. Experts date it to about 819 to 837. So it comes from the **Carolingian period**. It was drawn at **Reichenau** Abbey on an island in Lake Constance. Then it was sent to St Gallen. It consists of five pieces of **parchment** sewn together with thread.

The plan shows not only a church but a **whole monastery**. You can see living rooms for the monks, stables for animals, gardens and **workshops**. A school and rooms for guests and the sick are also drawn in. A monastery was supposed to make almost everything it needed itself. Largest and most exact is the **monastery church**, drawn with altars and measurements.

abschnitte.titel: A model, not a building plan
abschnitte.text: The monastery of St Gallen was not built exactly according to the plan. The plan was rather a **model** and an idea of what an ideal monastery could look like. The church built in St Gallen around 830 looked different. Even so the plan is very valuable. There is no older drawing of a monastery from the Middle Ages.
