The plan is kept today, well protected, in the **Abbey Library of St Gallen**. In **Messkirch** in Germany people are rebuilding a monastery according to the plan at **Campus Galli**. They work with old tools and methods as in the Middle Ages. In this way they want to find out how people built in those days.

gewusst: The Plan of St Gall is the oldest surviving drawing of a monastery from the Middle Ages.
At Campus Galli people work without modern machines.

teile.einleitung: The **Schengen Agreement** makes sure that people in Europe can travel across many borders without systematic checks on persons. Switzerland has been part of it since 2008, even though it does not belong to the European Union.
wichtigste: Schengen abolishes systematic checks on persons at internal borders.
The agreement was signed in 1985 in the village of Schengen in Luxembourg.
The Swiss people voted yes on 5 June 2005 with 54.6 per cent.
Schengen and Dublin are part of the Bilaterals II.
Since December 2008 Schengen has applied at Switzerland's land borders.
Customs checks still take place because Switzerland is not part of the EU customs union.

abschnitte.text: The agreement was signed in **1985** in the wine-growing village of **Schengen** in **Luxembourg**. The place lies on the Moselle, near the border with Germany and France. The idea was simple: anyone travelling within the **Schengen area** should no longer be systematically checked at the borders. **Spot checks** remain possible, however.

Switzerland negotiated with the EU a package of treaties, the **Bilaterals II**. They were signed in October 2004. They included **Schengen** and **Dublin**. Opponents of a closer link with the EU called a **referendum**. On **5 June 2005** the people voted yes with **54.6 per cent**.

From **12 December 2008** Switzerland applied Schengen at its **land borders**. At the **airports** this followed in March 2009. Since then there have been no systematic checks on persons at the borders with neighbouring countries. Because Switzerland is not part of the EU **customs union**, however, **goods** are still checked. That is why you still see customs officers at the border.

So that security is still guaranteed, the Schengen states work closely together. In the **Schengen Information System**, **SIS** for short, the police forces exchange alerts. For example, stolen cars or wanted persons are reported there. This replaces part of the former border checks.

Together with Schengen, the **Dublin Agreement** applies. It sets out which country has to examine an **asylum application**. Usually this is the state that a person first entered. This is meant to prevent someone from applying in several countries at the same time.

gewusst: Since Liechtenstein joined on 19 December 2011, all of Switzerland's neighbouring states belong to the Schengen area.
Norway and Iceland also belong to the Schengen area, even though they are not in the EU.

teile.einleitung: The Covenant of Stans was an agreement of the Confederate states of December 1481. It ended a dangerous quarrel between the cities and the rural states. At the same time Fribourg and Solothurn were taken into the Confederation.
wichtigste: The Covenant of Stans was decided in December 1481 at the Federal Diet in Stans.
A “Verkommnis” is an agreement or settlement.
Before that the cities and the rural states quarrelled, among other things over the Burgundian booty.
A war among the Confederates threatened.
Advice from Niklaus von Flüe helped bring about the agreement.
Fribourg and Solothurn became new states of the Confederation in 1481.

abschnitte.text: In the **Burgundian Wars** the Confederates defeated Duke Charles the Bold and captured great treasures. After that it was unclear how this **booty** should be shared. The cities such as **Zurich** and **Bern** quarrelled with the rural states such as **Uri** and **Schwyz**. It was also a question of who should have more power in the alliance.

In 1477 **Zurich**, **Bern** and **Lucerne** made a **civic alliance**, that is, a pact, with Fribourg and Solothurn. The rural states were annoyed about this. They feared that the cities would in this way get the majority in the alliance. The quarrel grew ever fiercer. In the end even a **war** between their own states seemed possible.

In December 1481 the envoys of the states met at the **Federal Diet** in **Stans**. The negotiations seemed to be failing. Then the priest of Stans, **Heimo Amgrund**, hurried to the **Ranft** to the hermit **Niklaus von Flüe**, who is called Brother Klaus. He came back with a message from the pious man. After that the envoys agreed.

In the **Covenant of Stans** the states agreed rules with each other. They promised not to attack one another and to stand together against uprisings. At the same time **Fribourg** and **Solothurn** were taken into the Confederation as new states. In this way a war among the Confederates was prevented. The alliance became firmer as a result.

gewusst: Niklaus von Flüe lived as a hermit in the Ranft and was later canonised.
With Fribourg in 1481 a state with many French-speaking people joined the alliance for the first time.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss National Exhibition of 1939, “Landi” for short, took place in Zurich. At a time full of danger of war it showed what makes Switzerland what it is. For many people it became an unforgettable experience.
wichtigste: The Landi took place in 1939 on both shores of Lake Zurich.
It opened on 6 May 1939 and ran until the end of October.
A cable car between two towers 75 metres high ran across the lake.
On the Schifflibach small boats travelled through the exhibition.
The Landi had over ten and a half million admissions.
For the Landi Hans Coray designed the famous aluminium Landi chair.

abschnitte.text: At the end of the 1930s a new war threatened in Europe. In Germany and Italy there were dictatorships. The Landi was meant to strengthen Switzerland's **unity** and show what makes the country special. In this connection people speak of **Spiritual National Defence**. The exhibition showed Switzerland's work, farming, technology, languages and traditions.

abschnitte.titel: On both shores of the lake
abschnitte.text: The Landi lay on both shores of **Lake Zurich**. One part was in **Wollishofen**, the other at the **Zürichhorn**. A **cable car** joined the two shores. It floated across the water between two towers 75 metres high and was the emblem of the Landi. On 6 May 1939 the exhibition opened its gates.

Especially popular was the **Schifflibach**. On this water channel small boats with six seats travelled through the exhibition, and a trip cost 50 centimes. Above the **Höhenstrasse** hung the flags of about 3,000 municipalities and of all the cantons. That showed the variety of Switzerland. The Landi had over ten and a half million paid admissions, more than twice as many as Switzerland had inhabitants.

On 1 September 1939 Germany invaded Poland and the **Second World War** began. The Swiss army was called up in the **general mobilisation**. The Landi therefore closed for three days and then reopened. It stayed open until the end of October 1939.

For the National Exhibition the designer **Hans Coray** designed a light chair made of **aluminium**. The seat has many holes in it. The chair is light, sturdy and weatherproof. It is still called the **Landi chair** today and counts as a classic of Swiss design.

gewusst: The Landi had more than twice as many admissions as Switzerland then had inhabitants.
The Landi chair is still made today.

teile.einleitung: The Swabian War was a short but important war in 1499. The Confederates and the people of the Grisons fought against the Swabian League and the House of Habsburg. Afterwards the Confederation in effect broke away from the Holy Roman Empire.
wichtigste: The Swabian War lasted from January to September 1499.
The opponents were the Swabian League and King Maximilian I of the House of Habsburg.
Important battles were Schwaderloh, the Calven and Dornach.
The war ended on 22 September 1499 with the Peace of Basel.
In Germany and Austria it is often called the Swiss War.
In 1501 Basel and Schaffhausen joined the Confederation.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages the Confederation belonged to the **Holy Roman Empire**. At the **Diet of Worms** in 1495 an imperial reform was decided. It created a supreme court, the **Imperial Chamber Court**, and a general imperial tax, the **Common Penny**. The Confederates refused to recognise either. As a result tensions with King **Maximilian I** grew.

The immediate cause was a dispute in the Grisons. The **League of God's House** and Habsburg Tyrol were quarrelling over rights in the **Val Müstair** and in the Vinschgau. The Grisons leagues had shortly before allied themselves with the Confederates. So at the beginning of 1499 the dispute grew into a great war. The opponents, besides the Habsburgs, were the **Swabian League**, an alliance of south German princes and cities.

On 11 April 1499 the Confederates won at **Schwaderloh** in Thurgau, south of Konstanz. In May the people of the Grisons defeated the Habsburg army in the **Battle of the Calven** in the Val Müstair. On 22 July 1499 came the decisive **Battle of Dornach** in what is now the canton of Solothurn. There too the Confederates won. After that peace negotiations soon began.

On 22 September 1499 the **Peace of Basel** was concluded. The Duke of Milan helped with the mediation. After this peace, the imperial court and imperial taxes in practice no longer applied to the Confederates. In this way the Confederation broke away from the Empire **in effect**. Legally, however, it only left the Empire in 1648.

After the war, towns near the border sought protection from the Confederates. In 1501 **Basel** and **Schaffhausen** joined the alliance. In this way the Confederation continued to grow. The Swabian War is therefore seen as an important step on the way to an independent Switzerland.

gewusst: Each side named the war after its opponent: “Schwabenkrieg” in Switzerland, “Schweizerkrieg” in southern Germany and Austria.
The whole war did not even last a year.

teile.einleitung: Paul Grüninger was a police commander in the canton of St Gallen. In 1938 and 1939 he saved the lives of several hundred Jewish refugees, even though he broke the rules in doing so.
wichtigste: Paul Grüninger was commander of the St Gallen cantonal police.
From 1938 many Jews fled from Austria to Switzerland.
Grüninger backdated the entry dates of the refugees.
In 1939 he was dismissed, in 1940 he was convicted.
In 1971 Yad Vashem honoured him as “Righteous Among the Nations”.
In 1995, after his death, a court acquitted him.

abschnitte.text: Paul Grüninger lived from 1891 to 1972. He was **commander of the St Gallen cantonal police**. In his youth he played football for **FC Brühl** in St Gallen. As police chief he was also responsible for the border with Austria. There he decided on the entry of many people.

In March 1938 **Austria** was annexed to the German Reich. Many Jews were persecuted there and tried to flee. Many crossed the border in the St Gallen Rhine Valley, especially near **Diepoldsau** over the Old Rhine. A refugee camp was also set up there. In August 1938 Switzerland closed the border to Jewish refugees.

Grüninger did not want to send the people back. In their papers he entered **dates of entry from before the border closure**. This way they counted as having entered legally and were allowed to stay. In this way he helped, as far as we know today, **several hundred** refugees. Without him they would have been sent back.

In **1939** Grüninger's help became known, and he was **dismissed**. He also lost his right to a pension. In **1940** the district court of St Gallen sentenced him to a fine for **breach of official duty and forgery of documents**. After that he lived for many years in poor circumstances.

In **1971** the memorial **Yad Vashem** in Jerusalem honoured him as **“Righteous Among the Nations”**. This title goes to people who saved Jews at great personal cost. Grüninger died in 1972 without having been rehabilitated. Only in **1995** did the district court of St Gallen overturn the old verdict and acquit him. Since **2006** the stadium of FC Brühl has been called the **Paul-Grüninger-Stadion**.

gewusst: The canton of St Gallen rehabilitated Grüninger politically in 1993, two years before the acquittal in court.
The stadium that bears his name belongs to the club where he himself played football.

teile.einleitung: The bull of Uri is the heraldic animal of the canton of Uri. In the yellow coat of arms you see a black bull's head with a red tongue and a red nose ring. It is one of the best known cantonal coats of arms in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The bull of Uri is black, the background yellow.
In the coat of arms you see only the bull's head.
It has two horns, a red tongue and a red nose ring.
The big war horn of the people of Uri was called the “Bull of Uri”.
The Harsthorn was used to give signals in battle.

abschnitte.titel: What the coat of arms looks like
abschnitte.text: The coat of arms of the canton of **Uri** shows a **black bull's head** on a **yellow** ground. You see only the head, so it is also called the **bull's head**. The bull has **two horns** like a real bull. It sticks out a **red tongue**. In its nose it wears a **red nose ring**. The strong colours make the coat of arms easy to recognise.

The people of Uri once had a great **Harsthorn**. That is a big **blowing horn** that makes a very loud note. It bore the name of the heraldic animal: **“Bull of Uri”**. In war it was blown to give loud **signals**. Its sound was meant to spur on their own warriors and frighten the enemy.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the name Uri come from?
abschnitte.text: According to an old explanation the name **Uri** is said to come from the **Ur**. The Ur, also called the **aurochs**, was a large **wild ox**. It once lived in the forests of Europe and is now extinct. Whether the name Uri really comes from the Ur is, however, **not certain**. The heraldic animal fits this old explanation well in any case.

gewusst: The bull of Uri can still be seen today on flags, number plates and letterheads of the canton of Uri.
The aurochs is an ancestor of our present day domestic cattle.

teile.einleitung: On 2 October 2001 all the aircraft of Swissair stayed on the ground. The proud airline had no money left. This event is called the Swissair grounding, and it was a great shock for Switzerland.
wichtigste: The grounding happened on 2 October 2001.
Swissair could no longer pay for fuel.
The Hunter strategy brought heavy losses.
Swissair belonged to the holding company SAirGroup.
The group's chief executive at the time was Mario Corti.
The new Swiss arose from Crossair in 2002.
From 2005 Lufthansa took over Swiss.

abschnitte.text: In the 1980s Swissair was very successful. It had so much money put by that it was called the **flying bank**. Swissair later belonged to the **SAirGroup**. This **holding company**, that is, an umbrella firm, also owned firms for in-flight meals, ground handling and other services. Nobody expected that this firm could ever go bust.

In the 1990s Swissair wanted to grow bigger. With the **Hunter strategy** it bought shares in many other airlines. “Hunter” is English and means someone who hunts. It was especially heavily involved in the Belgian **Sabena**, with 49.5 per cent. Many of these airlines, however, made big losses. So Swissair piled up huge **debts**.

In spring 2001 **Mario Corti** took over the leadership of the group. He tried to save the firm. On **2 October 2001**, however, the suppliers demanded cash payment and no longer fuelled the aircraft. All the Swissair aircraft had to stay on the ground. Many travellers were stranded at airports all over the world. In November 2001 Sabena too went bankrupt.

After the grounding the federal government helped with money so that flying could go on. The Basel based **Crossair**, a subsidiary of Swissair, was renamed. From it the new airline **Swiss** arose in 2002. It took over the most important routes and many aircraft. From 2005 the German **Lufthansa** took over Swiss. Swiss, however, still flies under its own name and with the Swiss cross to this day.

gewusst: A feature film about the grounding was made in 2006; it is called “Grounding”.
For many people in Switzerland the grounding was such a shock that they still know where they were that day.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss North Eastern Railway was the biggest private railway in eastern Switzerland in the 19th century. It came into being in 1853 and was shaped by Alfred Escher. In 1902 it was merged into the Swiss Federal Railways.
wichtigste: The North Eastern Railway arose in 1853 from the Northern Railway and the Zurich Lake Constance Railway.
Alfred Escher drove the merger forward.
The Spanisch-Brötli Railway of 1847 ran from Zurich to Baden.
The Railway Act of 1852 left railway building to private companies.
In 1880 the North Eastern Railway bought the network of the bankrupt National Railway.
On 1 January 1902 the North Eastern Railway, with 853 kilometres, passed to the SBB.

abschnitte.text: In 1844 the first railway reached Swiss soil: the line from **Strasbourg to Basel**. It ran almost entirely on French territory, however. In 1847 the first railway lying wholly in Switzerland was opened. It ran from **Zurich to Baden**. It was called the **Spanisch-Brötli Railway**, because it brought a pastry from Baden fresh to Zurich.

In 1852 Parliament passed a **Railway Act**. It left the building of the railways to **private companies**, which received a **concession** from the cantons. Supporters such as **Alfred Escher** had prevailed against building by the state. The result was a race between many private railways for the best routes.

abschnitte.titel: The North Eastern Railway is born
abschnitte.text: In 1853 the **Northern Railway**, the former Spanisch-Brötli Railway, and the **Zurich Lake Constance Railway** joined together. This created the **Swiss North Eastern Railway**. The merger was driven forward by Alfred Escher. The new company became the biggest private railway in eastern Switzerland. In 1875, together with the Central Railway, it opened the **Bözberg line** from Brugg to Pratteln, a direct link between Zurich and Basel.

From Winterthur the **Swiss National Railway** was promoted. As a “people's railway” it was meant to compete with the mighty North Eastern Railway. But the National Railway soon got into financial trouble and went **bankrupt**. In 1880 the North Eastern Railway bought its network for a fraction of the building costs. Many municipalities that had put money into the National Railway carried the debts for a long time.

In 1898 the people agreed to the federal government **buying back** the large private railways. On 1 January 1902 the North Eastern Railway passed to the **Swiss Federal Railways**. Its network then covered 853 kilometres. Many of its lines are still used today.

gewusst: The Spanisch-Brötli Railway is named after a pastry from Baden.
Alfred Escher also founded a large bank and campaigned for the Gotthard Railway.

teile.einleitung: The Villmergen Wars were two wars between Catholic and Reformed states of the Confederation. They took place in 1656 and 1712. They are named after Villmergen in Aargau, where the decisive battle took place each time.
wichtigste: Villmergen lies in the Freiamt in the canton of Aargau.
In the First Villmergen War in 1656 the Catholic states won.
In 1656 Zurich besieged Rapperswil without success.
The quarrel over the Toggenburg set off the war of 1712.
In 1712 the Reformed states won under the leadership of Bern and Zurich.
The Peace of Aarau ended the war in 1712.

abschnitte.text: Since the **Reformation** the Confederation had been split. There were **Catholic** and **Reformed** states. Both sides quarrelled over power and faith. Twice it came to war, and both times the decision fell at **Villmergen**. The village lies in the **Freiamt** in the canton of **Aargau**, near Wohlen.

In 1655 Reformed families secretly fled from **Arth** in the canton of Schwyz to Zurich. Schwyz punished relatives who had stayed behind. Thereupon **Zurich** declared war. Zurich troops besieged **Rapperswil** on Lake Zurich for several weeks, but the town held out. In January 1656 troops from **Lucerne** defeated the army of **Bern** at Villmergen. The **Catholic states** won, and their predominance was preserved.

The **Toggenburg** is a valley in today's canton of St Gallen. Its overlord at that time was the **Abbot of St Gallen**. The people of the Toggenburg resisted him. **Bern** and **Zurich** supported them, the Catholic states the abbot. From this arose in 1712 the **Second Villmergen War**. In July 1712 the Reformed states under the leadership of Bern won at Villmergen.

The war ended in 1712 with the **Peace of Aarau**, also called the **Fourth Landfriede**. The Catholic states lost the **County of Baden** and the **Lower Free Bailiwicks**. These territories went to Zurich, Bern and Glarus. In this way the people of Central Switzerland lost their land bridge between the Catholic states. In the common territories Reformed and Catholics were **given equal status**. The balance in the Confederation shifted in favour of the Reformed.

gewusst: After 1712 Baden lost its role as meeting place of the Federal Diet; later it met in Frauenfeld.
The Villmergen Wars were the last great wars of religion of the Old Confederation before the Sonderbund War of 1847.

teile.einleitung: Eastern Switzerland was once world-famous for its embroidery. Around 1910 embroidery was even Switzerland's most important export product. With the First World War this golden age collapsed abruptly.
wichtigste: St Gallen was already famous for its linen in the Middle Ages.
In 1828 Josua Heilmann invented the hand embroidery machine.
Many families embroidered at home as outwork in the villages.
Before the First World War embroidery enjoyed its greatest boom.
Around 1910 it made up about a sixth of Swiss exports.
After the war sales collapsed and there was great unemployment.
St Gallen lace is still used in fashion today.

abschnitte.text: Already in the **Middle Ages** and the early modern period **St Gallen** was famous for its **linen**. Linen is a cloth made from flax. It was sold to many countries in Europe. Later **cotton** was added. Finally **embroidery** became the most important textile trade in eastern Switzerland.

At first embroidery was done by hand. In **1828** **Josua Heilmann** from Mulhouse in Alsace invented the **hand embroidery machine**. With it one person could guide many needles at the same time. In eastern Switzerland the machine soon became widespread. Later even faster machines were added. This made it possible to produce far more embroidery.

A large part of the embroidery was produced as **outwork at home**. Many families in the **Appenzell region**, in **Thurgau** and in the **Toggenburg** embroidered at home on their own machines. Children often helped too. They took the finished goods to the **merchants** in St Gallen. From there they were sold all over the world.

Before the **First World War** embroidery enjoyed its greatest boom. Around **1910** it was Switzerland's most important **export product**. It made up about **16 to 18 per cent** of exports, that is, roughly a sixth. **St Gallen lace** became especially famous. These fine, openwork embroideries look like real lace.

With the **First World War** and new **fashions**, sales collapsed. Many customers abroad no longer bought embroidery. Tens of thousands of people in eastern Switzerland lost their jobs. There was great **unemployment**, and many embroidery machines were scrapped. Many people emigrated. Today some firms in St Gallen still make embroidery for fashion.

gewusst: Around 1910 Switzerland sold more embroidery abroad than any other product.
In the Textile Museum in St Gallen you can look at old embroidery and machines.

teile.einleitung: In 58 BC the **Helvetii** left their land in the area of present-day Switzerland and moved into Gaul. At **Bibracte** in present-day France the Roman general Julius Caesar stood in their way. The Helvetii lost the battle and had to return.
wichtigste: The battle took place in 58 BC.
Bibracte lies in Burgundy in present-day France.
Bibracte was the main town of the Aedui.
The Celtic town lay on Mont Beuvray.
The Romans under Caesar defeated the Helvetii.
According to Caesar, about 110,000 people returned home.

abschnitte.text: The Helvetii were a Celtic people on the Swiss Plateau. In **58 BC** they wanted to move west into Gaul with their families. The route through the Roman province was blocked to them. So with the permission of the **Sequani** they crossed the **Jura**. This had been arranged by the Aeduan **Dumnorix**, who according to Caesar was in league with the Helvetian nobleman **Orgetorix**.

Caesar followed the Helvetii with his legions. One sub-tribe, the **Tigurini**, had been left behind while crossing the **Saône**. Caesar surprised and defeated them there. Afterwards the aged leader **Divico** negotiated with Caesar. Divico had defeated a Roman army decades earlier, in 107 BC. The negotiations failed.

**Bibracte** was the largest **oppidum** of the **Aedui**. An oppidum is a **fortified Celtic town** with ramparts and walls. Bibracte lay on **Mont Beuvray** in **Burgundy**. The Aedui were allied with Rome at the time. Today there are excavations and a museum there.

Near Bibracte the great battle took place. The **Romans under Caesar** defeated the Helvetii after a long and hard fight. This meant the migration had failed. Caesar sent the survivors back to their homeland. He did not want the land to stay empty and Germanic peoples to move in. According to Caesar about **110,000** people returned.

Almost everything we know about these events comes from **Caesar** himself. He described the war in his work **“The Gallic War”**. In it Caesar also wanted to present his own deeds in a good light. So his figures should be treated with caution.

gewusst: According to Caesar, lists in Greek writing were found in the Helvetian camp on which all the emigrants had been counted.
After the defeat the Helvetii became allies of Rome and later lived under Roman rule.

teile.einleitung: The Schwarzenbach Initiative was a popular initiative that Switzerland voted on on 7 June 1970. It wanted to strictly limit the share of the foreign population. The vote moved the country like hardly any other.
wichtigste: The vote took place on 7 June 1970; at that time only men were allowed to vote.
It is named after the Zurich National Councillor James Schwarzenbach.
The share of foreigners was to be at most 10 per cent in each canton, and 25 per cent in Geneva.
The people and the cantons rejected the initiative.
Turnout was as high as it had not been since 1947.
In 1974 another “over-foreignisation” initiative was rejected with about two thirds against.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War the Swiss economy grew strongly. Factories, building sites and hotels needed many workers. So many people came to Switzerland from abroad, especially from **Italy**. Part of the population was worried about this development. The slogan **“Überfremdung”** (“over-foreignisation”) strongly shaped politics in the 1960s and 1970s.

Behind the initiative stood the Zurich National Councillor **James Schwarzenbach**. He sat in parliament for the **National Action** party. The initiative demanded that the share of foreigners in each canton be at most **10 per cent**. For **Geneva**, because of its many international organisations, an exception of 25 per cent was provided for. If it had been accepted, many foreign men and women would have had to leave Switzerland.

The **Federal Council**, the big parties and business rejected the initiative. They feared that many firms would have to close without foreign workers. That could have led to unemployment. The supporters, on the other hand, saw Switzerland's distinctive character as threatened. The debate was fought fiercely in many families and villages.

On 7 June 1970 very many men went to the polls; **women's suffrage** at federal level only existed from 1971. **Turnout** was as high as it had not been since 1947. The initiative was rejected by the people and the cantons. Even so, six cantons and two half-cantons voted in favour, including Bern, Fribourg and Lucerne. The result was closer than many had expected.

The subject remained important after 1970. In 1974 Switzerland voted on another **over-foreignisation initiative** from National Action. It demanded even sharper cuts than that of 1970. This initiative was clearly rejected with about two thirds against. The question of how much immigration Switzerland wants has occupied politics to this day.

gewusst: In 1970 only men were allowed to vote, even though the question affected everyone in the country.
The Schwarzenbach Initiative is regarded as one of the best-known votes in Swiss history.

teile.einleitung: On 2 March 1476 the Confederates defeated the army of Duke **Charles the Bold** of Burgundy at **Grandson** on Lake Neuchâtel. The battle is part of the Burgundian Wars and is famous for the huge spoils.
wichtigste: The Battle of Grandson took place on 2 March 1476.
Grandson is now in the canton of Vaud.
Charles had the Confederate garrison of Grandson executed.
The Confederates captured Charles's rich camp.
Part of the Burgundian spoils is shown in the Bernisches Historisches Museum.
The Battle of Murten followed in the same year.

abschnitte.text: **Charles the Bold** was Duke of **Burgundy**. He ruled over a rich territory that stretched from the Netherlands to the Jura. He wanted to enlarge his realm further. The Confederates, especially **Bern**, opposed him. This is how the **Burgundian Wars** began.

The Confederates had occupied **Grandson** Castle on **Lake Neuchâtel**. At the beginning of 1476 Charles besieged the castle with a large army. The Confederate garrison finally surrendered. Charles had the men **executed** anyway. This made the Confederates very **angry**, and they marched up with an army.

On **2 March 1476** the two armies met. The Confederates attacked with their **massed squares** (Gewalthaufen). Confusion broke out in the Burgundian army, and it **fled**. The losses in the battle itself were rather small. But Charles had to leave behind his whole **camp**.

The victors got their hands on **tents**, **cannon**, **jewellery**, valuable **tapestries** and a great deal of money. These **Burgundian spoils** were huge. Part of them can be seen today in the **Bernisches Historisches Museum**. The magnificent Burgundian tapestries are famous.

Charles did not give up and gathered a new army. In June 1476 he was beaten again at **Murten**. This gave rise to the well-known saying: **“At Grandson Charles lost his goods, at Murten his courage.”** Today Grandson belongs to the **canton of Vaud**. After the Burgundian Wars it was a common lordship of Bern and Fribourg.

gewusst: The saying is often continued: “at Nancy his blood”, because Charles fell there in 1477.
Grandson Castle still stands today and can be visited.

teile.einleitung: With the alliance of 1332 a city joined the forest cantons of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden for the first time. For the farmers of central Switzerland, Lucerne was the most important market and lay on the route to the Gotthard.
wichtigste: Lucerne was the first city in an alliance with the forest cantons.
The city was headed by a mayor, the Schultheiss.
At that time Lucerne belonged to the Habsburg domain.
In 1291 the Habsburgs bought Lucerne from Murbach Abbey.
Lucerne was the most important market town of the forest cantons.
Goods travelled by boat across the lake towards the Gotthard.
The Chapel Bridge was built around 1365.

abschnitte.titel: The first city in the alliance
abschnitte.text: **Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden** are called the **forest cantons**. They were rural valley communities with farmers and herdsmen. With **Lucerne**, a **city** joined the alliance for the first time in 1332. A city had walls, craftsmen, traders and a market. The alliance thus linked the countryside and the city.

abschnitte.titel: From the abbey to the Habsburgs
abschnitte.text: For a long time Lucerne belonged to **Murbach Abbey** in Alsace. In **1291** the abbey sold its rights over the city to the **Habsburgs**. So Lucerne was under Habsburg rule when it made the alliance. The alliance with the forest cantons was therefore a brave step for the people of Lucerne.

At the head of Lucerne's council stood a **Schultheiss**, a kind of mayor. He led the meetings and represented the city. The title also existed in other cities such as **Bern** and **Solothurn**. The citizens of the city arranged many things themselves. Over time the council became more and more powerful.

For the forest cantons, Lucerne was the most important **market town**. There the farmers sold their **cattle**, their cheese and other goods. In return they bought **grain** and **salt**, which were lacking in the mountains. The city also lay on the **Gotthard route**. So Lucerne was very important for trade with the south.

abschnitte.titel: Across the lake to the Gotthard
abschnitte.text: There were hardly any roads along the steep lakeshore in those days. So goods were taken by **boat** across Lake Lucerne to **Flüelen**. From there they continued by **pack animals** over the Gotthard. Around 1365 the **Chapel Bridge** was built in Lucerne. It was part of the fortifications and is one of the oldest covered wooden bridges in Europe.

gewusst: The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne is more than 650 years old.
The forest cantons also needed Lucerne for salt, which their valleys did not have.

teile.einleitung: The Neuchâtel Crisis was a dispute between Switzerland and Prussia in 1856 and 1857. It was about the question of whether Neuchâtel belonged to Switzerland or to the Prussian king. The conflict brought the country to the brink of war.
wichtigste: From 1815 Neuchâtel was a Swiss canton and at the same time a Prussian principality.
On 1 March 1848 republicans proclaimed the republic.
In September 1856 royalists occupied Neuchâtel Castle.
About 500 royalists were taken prisoner.
The Federal Assembly elected Guillaume-Henri Dufour as General.
On 26 May 1857 the Prussian king gave up Neuchâtel.

abschnitte.text: Since the **Congress of Vienna** Neuchâtel had been a Swiss **canton**. At the same time it still belonged to the **King of Prussia** as a **principality**. This double role was the root of the later conflict. On **1 March 1848** the radical-democratic **Montagnards** overthrew the royalist government. They proclaimed the **republic**. The Prussian king, however, maintained his claims.

In the night of **2 to 3 September 1856** supporters of the king occupied **Neuchâtel Castle**. They are called **royalists**. The castle was the seat of the government. The plan had been drawn up by Count Frédéric de Pourtalès-Steiger. But the republicans quickly won the castle back. About **500 royalists** were taken prisoner.

Prussia demanded the **release** of the prisoners. Switzerland wanted to free them only if the king gave up Neuchâtel. Prussia broke off diplomatic relations. On **27 December 1856** the Federal Assembly elected the experienced **Guillaume-Henri Dufour** as General. Switzerland sent troops to the **Rhine border**.

Emperor **Napoleon III** of France mediated between Switzerland and Prussia. The prisoners were released. Afterwards the great powers negotiated at a **conference in Paris**. For Switzerland, the envoy from Thurgau, **Johann Konrad Kern**, negotiated. In the treaty of **26 May 1857** King **Frederick William IV** gave up his rights to Neuchâtel.

gewusst: The Prussian king kept the title of Prince of Neuchâtel until his death in 1861, but Switzerland did not recognise this.
The Neuchâtel Crisis strengthened solidarity in the young federal state of 1848.

teile.einleitung: The National Council is the large chamber of the Swiss Parliament in Bern. Its 200 members represent the people and are elected every four years. Together with the Council of States, the National Council makes Switzerland's laws.
wichtigste: The National Council primarily represents the people.
It has 200 seats, which are shared among the cantons according to population.
Every canton has at least one seat; Zurich has the most seats.
The National Council is elected every four years, since 1919 by proportional representation.
At the first election in 1848 the National Council had 111 members.
In 1971 the first eleven women were elected to the National Council.
Parliament meets four times a year for ordinary sessions.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss Parliament is called the **Federal Assembly** and consists of two chambers. The **National Council** represents the people, the **Council of States** represents the cantons. Because the National Council, with 200 members, is much bigger than the Council of States, with 46, it is also called the **large chamber**. Both chambers are equally powerful: a law only applies if both agree.

The 200 seats are shared among the cantons according to **population**. The canton of Zurich has the most seats; since the 2023 elections it has 36. But every canton has at least one seat, so Uri, Glarus and the two Appenzells, for example, each have only one member. In elections each canton forms its own **constituency**.

The National Council is elected by the people every four years; the last election was in October 2023. Since 1919 **proportional representation** has applied, so the seats are shared out in proportion to the parties' votes. Voters can cross names off a list, write names twice (**cumulating**) or add people from other lists (**panachage**). Anyone who is a Swiss citizen and at least 18 years old may vote.

Parliament meets four times a year for ordinary **sessions**, each lasting three weeks. The members of the National Council debate laws, decide on the federal budget and oversee the government. Much of the work is done in **committees**, small groups that prepare business. Together with the Council of States they also elect the Federal Council, meeting as the United Federal Assembly.

The National Council has existed since the federal state was founded in 1848; the model for the two-chamber system was the USA. At the first election in 1848 it had 111 members, and later it grew with the population. Since 1963 the number of seats has been fixed at 200. In 1971, after the introduction of **women's suffrage**, the first eleven women were elected; in 2023 the share of women was about 39 per cent.

The National Council meets in the **Federal Palace** in Bern in a large chamber with a wall painting of Lake Lucerne. Each year it elects a new president. This person chairs the meetings and is seen as the **“highest Swiss”**. The meetings are public; you can follow them from the gallery or on the internet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of parliament that debates and votes separately.
An electoral system in which seats are shared out in proportion to the votes.
A sitting period of parliament lasting several weeks.
A group of members of parliament from the same or similar parties.
A small group of members of parliament who prepare business in depth.

gewusst: The members of the National Council are not professional politicians in the strict sense; many also have another job alongside.
The large wall painting in the National Council chamber shows the Rütli on Lake Lucerne, the place where, according to tradition, the Confederation began.

teile.einleitung: Le Corbusier was one of the most famous architects in the world. He was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds and built mainly in France. His ideas greatly changed the way people built in the 20th century.
wichtigste: Le Corbusier was an architect, painter and designer.
He was born in 1887 in La Chaux-de-Fonds in the canton of Neuchâtel.
His real name was Charles-Édouard Jeanneret.
He especially liked building with concrete.
Most of his buildings are in France.
He appeared on the 10-franc note of the eighth series.
On Lake Geneva he built the “Villa Le Lac” for his parents.

abschnitte.text: Le Corbusier was born in **1887** in **La Chaux-de-Fonds**. The town in the canton of Neuchâtel is known for its **watchmaking industry**. His real name was **Charles-Édouard Jeanneret**. At art school he first learned to decorate watch cases. A teacher encouraged him to become an architect. In his home town he built his first houses.

Later he moved to **Paris**. There he took the artist's name **Le Corbusier**. He lived in France for a long time and became a French citizen in 1930. Most of his buildings are in **France**. Well-known examples are the Villa Savoye near Paris and the chapel at Ronchamp. He even planned the city of Chandigarh in India.

Le Corbusier especially liked building with **concrete**. With it he could make smooth walls, flat roofs and large windows. His houses often stood on stilts so that there was free space underneath. He also invented his own system of measurement, the **Modulor**. It is based on the size of the human body.

In **Corseaux** on Lake Geneva he built a small house for his **parents**. It is called the **“Villa Le Lac”** and stands right on the shore. The house is long and narrow and has a long window with a view of the lake. Today you can visit it. There are also buildings in Geneva and Zurich that are linked to him.

In many photos Le Corbusier wears **round, dark glasses**. You can recognise him by them straight away. Switzerland honoured him on the yellow **10-franc note** of the eighth series, which was issued from 1995. Since 2016 several of his buildings have been part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**. The Villa Le Lac is one of them. Le Corbusier died in France in 1965.

gewusst: Le Corbusier was not only an architect, he also painted and designed furniture.
His buildings stand on three continents and some of them are UNESCO World Heritage sites.

teile.einleitung: For many decades Swissair was the national airline of Switzerland. Its aircraft with the Swiss cross on the tail flew all over the world. In 2001 its story ended with the grounding.
wichtigste: Swissair was founded in 1931.
It arose from the airlines Ad Astra Aero and Balair.
In 1934 Nelly Diener was the first air hostess in Europe.
From 1948 Swissair flew from Zurich Kloten Airport.
From 1960 it used jet aircraft.
On 2 October 2001 all the aircraft stayed on the ground.
Swissair was followed by the airline Swiss.

abschnitte.text: In 1931 two smaller Swiss airlines joined together: **Ad Astra Aero** and **Balair**. From them **Swissair** arose. At the start it had only a few small aircraft. The flights led mainly to cities in Europe. Flying was expensive then and something for only a few people.

In 1934 Swissair took on **Nelly Diener**. She looked after the passengers on board, brought drinks and helped with questions. That made her the **first flight attendant in Europe**. Today this job exists at every large airline. Nelly Diener became known throughout Switzerland as a result.

In the first years Swissair took off from **Dübendorf airfield** near Zurich. In 1948 it moved to the new **Zurich Kloten Airport**. There were longer runways there for bigger aircraft. From **1960** Swissair flew with **jet aircraft**, also called jets. These were much faster than propeller aircraft and flew, for example, to London and New York.

On the red tail of the aircraft shone a white **Swiss cross**. In this way Swissair was recognised at every airport in the world. The company was regarded as very reliable and punctual. Many people in Switzerland were proud of “their” airline. For many it was a piece of home abroad.

At the end of the 1990s Swissair made heavy losses. On **2 October 2001** it had no money left to pay, for example, for fuel. All the aircraft had to stay on the ground. This event is called the **grounding**. From the regional airline **Crossair** the new airline **Swiss** then arose, which took over many aircraft and routes.

gewusst: Swissair existed for exactly 70 years, from 1931 to 2001.
The word “grounding” comes from English and means roughly “keeping on the ground”.

teile.einleitung: In the Ancien Régime, that is, before 1798, only a few noble families ruled in some Swiss cities. These families are called **patricians** and their rule the patriciate.
wichtigste: Patricians were a few noble families who ruled a city.
Typical patrician cities were Bern, Lucerne, Fribourg and Solothurn.
Only families “fit to govern” (regimentsfähig) were allowed to hold government offices.
The ruling gentlemen were often called “Gracious Lords”.
In guild cities such as Zurich the councils were chosen through the guilds.
In 1798 the French invasion ended the rule of the patricians.

abschnitte.text: A **patriciate** is the rule of a few old and wealthy families over a city and its land. In the Old Confederation such cities were found above all in **Bern**, **Lucerne**, **Fribourg** and **Solothurn**. So people speak of **patrician cities**. The families sat on the councils for generations. The people in the countryside were subjects and had hardly any say.

Not every citizen was allowed to govern. Only members of families that were **fit to govern** (regimentsfähig) could be elected to the **Great** and **Small Council**. “Fit to govern” thus means: entitled to take on government offices. In the 17th and 18th centuries **citizenship** was practically closed. New families were hardly admitted any more, and families that had died out were not replaced. So the circle of the powerful grew ever smaller.

The ruling councils were often called **“Gracious Lords”**. The title shows how they placed themselves above their subjects as the authorities. In Bern there was even the **Outer Estate**. This was an association of young patricians who practised governing with offices of their own. In this way the sons prepared for their later tasks in the state.

Patricians did not rule everywhere. In **guild cities** such as Zurich, Basel or Schaffhausen the councils were chosen through the **guilds**, that is, through the associations of craftsmen and merchants. But even there a small upper class of a few families formed over time. In the patrician cities, by contrast, the guilds had hardly any political influence.

In **1798** **French troops** marched into Switzerland, and the Old Confederation collapsed. The new **Helvetic Republic** abolished the privileges of the patricians. All citizens were to be equal before the law. After 1815 old families did partly return to power, but the old order never fully came back.

gewusst: In the 18th century only a few dozen families still ruled Bern, the largest city-state north of the Alps.
The Outer Estate in Bern even had its own Schultheiss (mayor).

teile.einleitung: A **Reisläufer** was a Swiss mercenary who fought in foreign armies for pay. From the 15th to the 18th century very many young men from the Confederation went off to foreign wars.
wichtigste: Reisläufer were mercenaries in foreign service.
“Reise” used to mean a military campaign.
Many men went because there was little work at home.
The Confederates fought in the Gewalthaufen (massed square) with pikes about 5 metres long.
Foreign princes paid pensions to states and politicians.
Ulrich Zwingli fought against Reislaufen in Zurich.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from **“Reise”**. In the Middle Ages this meant a **military campaign**. Anyone who “ran into the Reise” went off to war. Reisläufer fought as **mercenaries** for foreign rulers, for example for the King of France, the Pope or princes in Italy. For this they received **pay**, that is, a wage.

Many valleys in the Confederation were **poor** and could not feed all their people. There was little work and little to earn. The pay and the hope of **plunder** lured young men into foreign armies. Foreign princes also paid **pensions** to the states and to influential men so that they were allowed to recruit mercenaries.

The Confederates fought in the **Gewalthaufen**. This was a dense block of warriors with **pikes** that were about **5 metres** long. Inside stood fighters with **halberds**. In this way they could repel attacks by horsemen. At the very front fought **double-pay soldiers** (Doppelsöldner), for example with the two-handed sword. Because their task was especially dangerous, they received double pay.

Emperor **Maximilian I** encouraged south German mercenaries, the **Landsknechte**. They took over the tactics and weapons of the Confederates. There was bitter enmity between Landsknechte and Reisläufer. In Italy they often faced each other on opposite sides.

The Zurich reformer **Ulrich Zwingli** had himself experienced the horrors of the mercenary wars. He sharply condemned Reislaufen and pensions. Even so, many Swiss still served in foreign regiments until the 19th century. The federal state finally banned recruitment. Today the **Pontifical Swiss Guard** is the only permitted exception.

gewusst: Even though Reisläufer fought for foreign lords, it sometimes happened that Swiss soldiers stood on both sides of a battle.
The reputation of Swiss mercenaries was so good that in 1506 the Pope founded his own Swiss Guard.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss National Bank is the central bank of Switzerland. It issues the banknotes and makes sure the franc stays stable. In the Second World War it bought a lot of gold from Germany, which was later fiercely criticised.
wichtigste: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) is the central bank of Switzerland.
It issues the banknotes and is meant to ensure stable prices.
In the Second World War the franc could be freely exchanged and was accepted worldwide.
The National Bank bought large amounts of gold from the German Reichsbank, including looted gold.
According to the Bergier Commission about three quarters of the Reichsbank's gold deliveries abroad went through Switzerland.
In 1997 a special fund was created for needy Holocaust survivors.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Bank**, SNB for short, began its work in 1907. It has seats in **Bern** and **Zurich**. Only it may issue **banknotes** in Switzerland. Its most important task is **monetary policy**: it is meant to make sure that prices stay stable. A bank like this is called a **central bank**.

In the **Second World War** the Swiss franc was one of the few currencies that could be freely exchanged. It was accepted worldwide. With francs Germany could buy important **raw materials** in neutral countries such as Portugal or Spain. The **German Reichsbank** therefore exchanged gold for francs in Switzerland. The National Bank played the main part in this.

Part of the gold was **looted gold**. Germany had stolen it from occupied countries and from persecuted people. According to the **Bergier Commission** about 77 per cent of the Reichsbank's gold deliveries abroad went through Switzerland. After the war the National Bank said it had bought the gold **in good faith** and had behaved neutrally. The Commission countered that those responsible could have known early on where it came from.

In the 1990s Switzerland's role in the Second World War was strongly criticised internationally. The federal government therefore set up a commission of experts, named after its chairman **Jean-François Bergier**. It investigated Switzerland's relations with Germany during the war. In 1997 the **Special Fund for Needy Victims of the Holocaust and Shoah** was created. Banks, business and the National Bank paid money into it.

gewusst: The National Bank is the only body allowed to issue banknotes in Switzerland.
The Bergier Commission published its findings in many volumes.

teile.einleitung: The Colonels' Affair was a scandal in the First World War. Two senior Swiss officers passed secret information to Germany and Austria-Hungary. The case deepened the divide between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland.
wichtigste: At the centre were Colonels Karl Egli and Moritz von Wattenwyl.
They passed on secret daily bulletins of the General Staff.
The information went to the military attachés of the Central Powers.
The cryptographer André Langie set the case in motion.
In February 1916 the colonels were acquitted of criminal charges in Zurich.
General Wille punished both with 20 days of arrest each.
French-speaking Switzerland felt the verdict was far too mild.

abschnitte.text: In the **First World War** Switzerland was **neutral**. It was not allowed to favour any side in the war. Colonels **Karl Egli** and **Friedrich Moritz von Wattenwyl** worked in the **General Staff**. They passed on the secret **daily bulletins**, that is, the daily situation reports. They also passed on deciphered telegrams. In doing so they violated neutrality.

The information went to the **military attachés** of Germany and Austria-Hungary. A military attaché is an officer who works at an embassy abroad. Germany and Austria-Hungary were called the **Central Powers**. They were fighting against France, Britain and Russia. This angered above all **French-speaking Switzerland**, which was friendly towards France.

In 1915 the cryptographer **André Langie** cracked a Russian **secret code**. A cryptographer is an expert in secret writing. Langie noticed that dispatches referred to Swiss General Staff reports. He suspected **treason**. So he informed the National Councillor from Vaud, **Édouard Secretan**.

In **February 1916** the two colonels came before the **divisional court** in Zurich. The court **acquitted** them of criminal charges. The case went back to the military authorities for judgement on disciplinary matters. General **Ulrich Wille** punished both with **20 days of arrest** each. The Federal Council also removed them from their posts.

French-speaking newspapers sharply criticised the mild verdict. Many in **French-speaking Switzerland (Romandie)** saw it as proof of a **pro-German army leadership**. In German-speaking Switzerland, by contrast, the case was rather played down. This created a **crisis of confidence** in the army and the government. The **divide** between the parts of the country grew deeper.

gewusst: A code-breaker brought the scandal to light because he deciphered a Russian secret code.
The two colonels were acquitted by the court and punished only on disciplinary grounds.

teile.einleitung: Matthäus Schiner was Bishop of Sion and a cardinal. Around 1500 he was one of the most influential politicians in the Confederation. He fought with all his strength against French influence in Italy.
wichtigste: Matthäus Schiner came from the Goms in the Valais.
In 1499 he became Bishop of Sion.
Pope Julius II made him a cardinal in 1511.
In 1512 he led the Confederates to join the Holy League against France.
His great opponent in the Valais was Georg Supersaxo.
In 1519 he supported the election of Charles V as king.
He died of the plague in Rome in 1522.

abschnitte.text: Matthäus Schiner was born around **1465** in Mühlebach near Ernen in the **Goms**. At that time the Valais was divided into districts called **Zenden**. Schiner came from a simple background. He rose through the **Church**. He was clever, a good speaker and very ambitious.

abschnitte.titel: Bishop and ruler of the land
abschnitte.text: In **1499** Schiner became **Bishop of Sion**. The bishop was not only a spiritual shepherd. He was also **count and prefect of the Valais** and so a worldly ruler. The bishops traced this power back to a supposed gift from Charlemagne, the **“Carolina”**. But they were constantly quarrelling over power with the Zenden.

abschnitte.titel: Cardinal in the service of the Pope
abschnitte.text: Schiner was a determined opponent of **France**. Pope **Julius II** wanted to drive the French out of Italy. Schiner helped him to win the Confederates for the **Holy League**. For this the Pope made him a **cardinal** in **1511**. In 1512 the Confederates marched into Italy in the **Pavia Expedition**. The same Pope had founded the **Swiss Guard** in 1506.

**Georg Supersaxo** was a powerful politician in the Valais. At first he helped Schiner onto the bishop's throne. Later he changed to the **French camp**. The two became bitter enemies. Their struggle for power divided the Valais for many years. At times Schiner even had to flee from the Valais.

After the defeat at **Marignano** in 1515 Schiner continued his fight against France. In **1519** he supported the election of the Habsburg **Charles V** as King of the Romans and Germans. Charles was elected against the French king Francis I. After the death of Pope Leo X, Schiner stayed in **Rome**. There he died in **1522** of the **plague**.

gewusst: At one point Schiner was even talked about as a possible pope.
The Pope who made Schiner a cardinal also founded the Swiss Guard.

teile.einleitung: **Looted gold** is the name for gold that Nazi Germany had stolen from other countries and people in the Second World War. Part of it was sold to Switzerland. After the war it was negotiated over and later discussed for a long time.
wichtigste: In the Second World War the German Reichsbank sold a great deal of gold to Switzerland.
Part of it was stolen, for example Belgian central bank gold.
The Reichsbank melted down looted gold and backdated it to disguise its origin.
In the Washington Agreement of 1946 Switzerland paid 250 million francs.
Walter Stucki led the Swiss delegation.
In the 1990s the subject was investigated afresh.

abschnitte.text: In the Second World War Germany needed **foreign currency**, that is, other countries' money, to buy raw materials and goods. Switzerland was neutral, and the **franc** was a sought-after currency. So the German **Reichsbank** sold a lot of gold to the **Swiss National Bank** and to commercial banks. Part of this gold was stolen.

In occupied countries Germany had seized the gold reserves of the central banks, such as the gold of the **Belgian** central bank. The Reichsbank had such gold **melted down** and stamped the bars with false, earlier years such as 1938. This was so that nobody would recognise where it came from. **Melmer gold** is the name for valuables that the SS had stolen from the victims of the concentration camps. It is named after the SS officer Bruno Melmer, who delivered this loot to the Reichsbank.

After the war the Allies demanded that Switzerland account for itself. The diplomat **Walter Stucki** negotiated in Washington with the USA, Britain and France. On **25 May 1946** the **Washington Agreement** was signed. Switzerland paid **250 million francs** for the reconstruction of Europe, without acknowledging any legal obligation. In return the Allies waived further claims over the gold purchases.

The agreement also regulated the assets of people in Germany that were held in Switzerland. These had been frozen since February 1945. Switzerland was to **record and liquidate** them, that is, register and sell them. The proceeds were to go half to Switzerland and half to the reconstruction of Europe.

In the 1990s the subject came back into the headlines, partly because of money belonging to victims that lay in Swiss banks. The federal government set up an independent commission of historians, the **Bergier Commission**. It examined Switzerland's role in the Second World War closely. Its reports showed that the National Bank had had early indications of stolen gold.

gewusst: The Bergier Commission is named after its president, the historian Jean-François Bergier.
Gold is easy to melt down, so its origin is often hard to prove.

teile.einleitung: Maggi is a well-known brand of soups, stock and seasoning. It was founded by the Swiss man Julius Maggi. He wanted to make quick and nourishing meals possible for factory workers.
wichtigste: Julius Maggi was born in Frauenfeld in 1846.
He founded the company Maggi.
The factory stood in Kemptthal near Winterthur.
He made his first soup powders from pulses.
He wanted cheap, nourishing food for factory workers.
In 1908 the Maggi stock cube came onto the market.
Maggi seasoning has been sold in a brown bottle since 1886.

abschnitte.text: **Julius Maggi** was born in **1846** in **Frauenfeld** in the canton of Thurgau. Later he took over a **mill**. In the age of industrialisation many people worked in factories. They had long working days, little time and little money. Julius Maggi wanted to help them eat well.

For his first **soup powders** Maggi used flour made from **peas, beans and lentils**. These **pulses** are rich in **protein** and fill you up. The soups were cheap and quick to cook. So even **factory workers** could eat a warm and nourishing meal. The idea went down well at the time.

**Maggi seasoning** has existed since **1886**. A few drops give soups and other dishes more flavour. The seasoning comes in a **brown bottle** with a yellow and red label. This bottle has remained almost unchanged to this day. Many people recognise it straight away.

In **1908** the **Maggi stock cube** came onto the market. You dissolve it in hot water and get a **bouillon**, that is, a clear broth. The cube is small, keeps for a long time and is easy to transport. It became a great success all over the world.

Julius Maggi's factory stood in **Kemptthal** near Winterthur in the canton of Zurich. Many people worked there. The company grew quickly and also built factories abroad. Julius Maggi died in 1912. Later the company became part of the **Nestlé** group.

gewusst: The Maggi bottle has looked almost the same for more than 100 years.
Maggi began with soups made from peas, beans and lentils.

teile.einleitung: The Sonderbund was a defensive alliance of seven Catholic conservative cantons, founded in 1845. The liberal majority of the cantons held it to be forbidden, and because of this the Sonderbund War broke out in 1847. After it the modern Swiss federal state arose in 1848.
wichtigste: The Sonderbund was founded in 1845.
It consisted of seven cantons, including Lucerne.
The members were Catholic and conservative.
Their opponents were the Liberals and Radicals.
The leading figure was the Lucerne politician Konstantin Siegwart-Müller.
In July 1847 the Federal Diet decided by a narrow majority to dissolve the Sonderbund.
In November 1847 the Sonderbund was defeated in the Sonderbund War.

abschnitte.text: The **Sonderbund** was an alliance of seven cantons: Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Zug, Fribourg and Valais, Obwalden and Nidwalden counting together as Unterwalden. They were Catholic and conservative. They wanted to protect their faith and their independence against the Liberals. Ticino was also Catholic, but did not belong to it.

In 1841 the canton of Aargau abolished its **monasteries**, which greatly angered the Catholics. In 1844 Lucerne brought the order of the **Jesuits** to its higher schools. That in turn angered the Liberals. The two camps mistrusted each other more and more.

In 1844 and 1845 armed groups of Liberals marched against Lucerne. They are called **Freischaren** (free corps). Both expeditions failed, and there were deaths. After that the Catholic conservative cantons joined together in 1845 to form the Sonderbund, led by Konstantin Siegwart-Müller.

The majority of the **Federal Diet** held the Sonderbund to be impermissible, because it broke the Federal Treaty of 1815. In July 1847 it decided by a narrow majority to dissolve it. The Sonderbund cantons refused. The Federal Diet thereupon raised an army under General **Guillaume Henri Dufour**.

In November 1847 the **Sonderbund War** lasted only just under four weeks. The Confederate troops first took Fribourg and then Lucerne. Dufour ordered that the wounded and prisoners be treated humanely. There were just under a hundred deaths, far fewer than in other civil wars.

After the victory of the Liberals the first **Federal Constitution** was adopted in 1848. The loose league of states became a federal state with a Federal Council and a Parliament. The losers were soon brought back into the new state. The Sonderbund War was the last war on Swiss soil.

begriffe.erklaerung: An attitude that wants to keep what has proved its worth and to preserve traditions.
A Catholic order that takes special care of schools and education.
Armed volunteers who fight without orders from the state.
The assembly of the envoys of all the cantons before 1848.

gewusst: General Dufour, who led the Sonderbund War, later belonged to the founders of the Red Cross.
The Sonderbund War lasted less than a month and was the last war on Swiss soil.

teile.einleitung: In 1653 farmers in several states of the Old Confederation rose up against the ruling cities. It was the biggest uprising of the rural population in the Old Confederation. In the end the cities prevailed.
wichtigste: The Swiss Peasants' War broke out in 1653.
It began in the Entlebuch and spread to Bern, Solothurn and Basel.
One of the triggers was the devaluation of the Batzen coins.
The most important leader was Niklaus Leuenberger from Rüderswil.
In June 1653 the farmers were defeated at Wohlenschwil.
Leuenberger was executed in Bern and Christian Schybi in Sursee.

abschnitte.text: During the **Thirty Years' War** (1618 to 1648) Swiss farmers were able to sell their products well. After the war prices fell sharply. Many farmers had debts. In addition, Bern and Lucerne devalued their **Batzen coins**. In December 1652 the copper Batzen in Bern lost half their value and could be exchanged for only three days. Many farmers thus lost a large part of their savings.

First the farmers in the **Entlebuch** rose against the city of **Lucerne**. Soon the uprising spread to the subject territories of **Bern**, **Solothurn** and **Basel**. The farmers demanded lower dues and more rights. They turned against the power of the ruling cities, which ruled over the countryside.

**Niklaus Leuenberger** from Rüderswil in the Emmental was elected spokesman of the farmers. He led the negotiations with the cities. In May 1653 farmers from several states made the **Huttwil League** in Huttwil. They swore to help each other. The authorities saw in it a dangerous conspiracy against their rule.

The **Federal Diet**, the assembly of the Confederate states, raised an army against the farmers. Under the Zurich General **Werdmüller** the farmers were defeated in June 1653 at **Wohlenschwil** in Aargau. After that the uprising quickly collapsed. The authorities of Bern, Lucerne, Solothurn and Basel had prevailed.

After the war the leaders were punished harshly. Niklaus Leuenberger was captured and **executed** in Bern in September 1653. **Christian Schybi** from Escholzmatt, the military leader of the Entlebuch men, was executed in Sursee. The cities wanted to deter further uprisings in this way. Today monuments recall the peasant leaders.

gewusst: For many farmers the devaluation of the coins was as if their savings had been halved overnight.
The Peasants' War affected four Confederate states at the same time: Lucerne, Bern, Solothurn and Basel.

teile.einleitung: Mobilisation means that a country calls up its army and makes it ready to fight. In Switzerland general wartime mobilisation began on 2 September 1939, shortly after the German attack on Poland. Hundreds of thousands of men left their families and jobs and did active service until 1945 to protect the country.
wichtigste: At the end of August 1939 the Federal Council first called up the border troops.
General wartime mobilisation began on 2 September 1939.
About 430,000 soldiers and a further 200,000 or so auxiliary service personnel were called up.
In the Women's Auxiliary Service over 20,000 women at times served voluntarily.
Swiss soldiers did on average about 800 days of active service.
From 1940 the wage and income compensation scheme replaced the lost wages of the men serving.
About 4,000 Swiss soldiers died during active service.

abschnitte.text: In a **mobilisation** an army's soldiers are called away from civilian life to serve. Switzerland has a **militia army**, so the soldiers normally work in their jobs and only report for periods of service. In an emergency they have to appear at their assembly points within a short time. Switzerland had already mobilised its army in the First World War in 1914, at that time under General Ulrich Wille.

As war threatened, the Federal Council first called up the **border troops** at the end of August 1939. On 30 August 1939 the Federal Assembly elected **Henri Guisan** as General. On 2 September 1939, one day after the German attack on Poland, general wartime mobilisation began. About 430,000 soldiers reported for duty, and about 200,000 auxiliary service personnel were added.

In 1939 the **Women's Auxiliary Service** (FHD) was founded, in which at times over 20,000 women worked voluntarily for the army. They worked, for example, as radio operators, cooks or in aircraft spotting. At home, women, children and older people had to take over the men's work on farms and in shops. From 1940 the **wage and income compensation scheme** replaced the lost wages of the men serving. It is seen as the forerunner of the AVS (old-age insurance).

In May and June 1940 German aircraft repeatedly violated Swiss airspace. In the process the Swiss **air force** shot down 11 German aircraft and lost 3 of its own. Germany reacted with sharp protests and threats. On 20 June 1940, under German pressure, General Guisan forbade the air force to fight air battles over Switzerland.

After the defeat of France in 1940 part of the troops were released again. After that the army kept up its strength mostly through about 80 **partial mobilisations**, in which units relieved each other. On 25 July 1940, at the **Rütli Report**, Guisan explained to his officers the strategy of the **Réduit**, a defence in the Alps. On average each soldier did about 800 days of active service.

During active service from 1939 to 1945 about 4,000 Swiss soldiers died, mainly in accidents and from illness. For **treason**, 17 Swiss were sentenced to death and executed. Active service ended on 20 August 1945. For many families the time of mobilisation was a formative memory of hardship and solidarity.

begriffe.erklaerung: Calling up the army so that it is ready for action.
Military service in an emergency, when the country is under threat.
An army of citizens who do military service alongside their jobs.
The defensive position of the Swiss army in the Alps in the Second World War.
Service for people who did not fight as soldiers but supported the army.

gewusst: Switzerland only has a general in wartime or in times of great danger; Henri Guisan was one of only four generals in the history of the federal state.
The wage compensation scheme of 1940 was so successful that it served as a model for the AVS (old-age insurance) of 1948.

teile.einleitung: The Sechseläuten is the big spring festival of the city of Zurich. The high point is the burning of the Böögg, a big snowman. With it winter is symbolically driven out.
wichtigste: The Sechseläuten is a spring festival of the Zurich guilds.
It usually takes place on the third Monday in April.
The Böögg is a snowman made of cotton wool and stands for winter.
At 6 pm the woodpile under the Böögg is lit.
The faster the head explodes, the finer the summer is supposed to be.
The Böögg burns on the Sechseläutenplatz near Bellevue.

abschnitte.text: The **Sechseläuten** is a festival of the **guilds** of the city of Zurich. Guilds were once associations of craftsmen and merchants. In summer a bell at six o'clock in the evening rang in the end of work. That is where the name Sechseläuten (“six o'clock ringing”) comes from. To this day the woodpile is lit at **6 pm**.

The **Böögg** is a big snowman made of cotton wool. It stands high up on a woodpile. The Böögg is a symbol of **winter**. When it burns, winter is driven away. The festival usually takes place on the **third Monday in April**.

abschnitte.titel: What will the summer be like?
abschnitte.text: In the Böögg's head there are **bangers**. Everyone waits excitedly until the head explodes. The faster that happens, the finer the **summer** is supposed to be, people say. Many people time it exactly. That is of course no real weather forecast, but a fun custom.

Before the fire the guilds march through the city in old costumes. On the day before there is a **children's parade** of its own. When the woodpile is burning, the **guild members** ride round the fire on horses at a gallop. This takes place on the **Sechseläutenplatz** near Bellevue, close to Lake Zurich. Thousands of people watch.

gewusst: The time until the Böögg's head explodes is measured every year and reported in the media.
The Sechseläutenplatz is named after the festival.

teile.einleitung: St Gallen embroidery once made eastern Switzerland world famous. Fine patterns of thread on cloth were sold all over the world. Around 1910 embroidery was even the most important export product of Switzerland.
wichtigste: In embroidery patterns are sewn on cloth with needle and thread.
Eastern Switzerland around St Gallen was world famous for fine embroidery.
In the 19th century more and more embroidery was done by machine.
Isaak Gröbli invented the shuttle embroidery machine in 1863.
Around 1910 embroidery, with about 18 per cent of exports, was the biggest export branch.
In the Textile Museum St Gallen you can look at old embroideries.

abschnitte.text: In **embroidery** patterns are sewn on a cloth with needle and thread. In this way flowers, tendrils and fine decorations are made. Embroideries and **lace** adorned dresses, blouses and linen. For a long time embroidery was done only by hand. That was very laborious work, often done as home work in the farmhouses of eastern Switzerland.

In the 19th century more and more embroidery was done with **embroidery machines**. In this way much more could be made. In 1863 **Isaak Gröbli** from eastern Switzerland invented the **shuttle embroidery machine**. It caught on only gradually. In 1879 the firm **Gebrüder Iklé** put the first shuttle embroidery machine in the city of St Gallen into operation. With that the heyday of factory embroidery began.

The embroideries from eastern Switzerland went to America, England, France and many other countries. About 95 per cent were sold abroad. Around 1910 embroidery, with about 18 per cent of exports, was the **biggest export branch** of Switzerland. Shortly before the **First World War** the industry reached its peak. Many people in the region lived from it.

After the First World War fashion changed and demand collapsed. Many embroidery firms had to close, and many people lost their jobs. Some firms survived, however. To this day firms in eastern Switzerland make fine fabrics for **fashion**. In the **Textile Museum St Gallen** you can look at lace and embroideries from many centuries.

gewusst: Around 1910 embroidery was the most important export product of the whole of Switzerland.
Almost the whole production went abroad.

teile.einleitung: The Matterhorn near Zermatt is one of the best-known mountains in the world. Its first ascent in 1865 was a great success and at the same time a tragic accident. It was also in this period that tourism began in the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: The Matterhorn was first climbed on 14 July 1865.
The roped party was led by the Englishman Edward Whymper.
The group climbed from Zermatt via the Hörnli Ridge.
On the descent four of the seven climbers were killed.
Three days later Jean-Antoine Carrel reached the summit from the Italian side.
In 1863 the Swiss Alpine Club was founded in Olten.
In 1871 the Rigi Railway ran as the first rack railway in Europe.

abschnitte.text: The **Matterhorn** stands on the border between Switzerland and Italy. For a long time it was thought to be almost impossible to climb. The Englishman **Edward Whymper**, an illustrator and mountaineer, tried several times without success. His rival was the mountain guide **Jean-Antoine Carrel** from Valtournenche in Italy. Both were determined to be the first.

On **14 July 1865** a roped party of **seven** climbers reached the summit. They climbed from **Zermatt** via the **Hörnli Ridge**. This ridge is now the normal route from the Swiss side. It starts at the **Hörnli Hut** at 3,260 metres. Shortly before the summit Whymper and his guide unroped and hurried up first.

On the way down, **four** men fell down the north face: Croz, Hadow, Hudson and Douglas. The **rope** to the other three broke. So Whymper and two mountain guides survived. The accident became known all over Europe. The date is seen as the end of the **“Golden Age”** of alpinism, in which many great Alpine peaks were climbed for the first time.

Only **three days** after the first ascent, **Jean-Antoine Carrel** also reached the summit. He climbed from Italy via the **Lion Ridge**. For years he had competed with Whymper for the first victory on the summit. Today there are several routes up the Matterhorn.

In this period the Alps became more and more popular with travellers. In **1863** the **Swiss Alpine Club** was founded in **Olten**. It built huts and promoted the exploration of the mountains. In **1871** the **Rigi Railway** ran from Vitznau as the first rack railway in Europe. In **St Moritz** the hotelier **Johannes Badrutt** invited English summer guests in 1864 to come back in winter. This was the start of **winter tourism**.

gewusst: Badrutt promised his guests sunshine in winter, and the guests stayed until Easter.
The Matterhorn is about 4,478 metres high.

teile.einleitung: The League of Nations was an organisation of states that was meant to secure peace after the First World War. Its seat was in Geneva. Switzerland joined it in 1920 after a popular vote.
wichtigste: The US President Woodrow Wilson suggested its founding.
The League of Nations began its work in Geneva in 1920.
Switzerland joined on 16 May 1920 after a popular vote.
The cantons' majority was very narrow, at 11½ to 10½.
In 1936 the League of Nations moved into the Palais des Nations.
In 1938 Switzerland returned to full neutrality.
In 1946 the League of Nations was dissolved.

abschnitte.text: The **First World War** brought great suffering to Europe. The US President **Woodrow Wilson** called in 1918, in his **Fourteen Points**, for a league of nations. The states were to settle disputes together and peacefully. So the **League of Nations** came into being. In 1920 it began its work. As its seat it chose **Geneva**.

In Switzerland the people and the cantons decided on joining. On **16 May 1920** **56.3 per cent** said Yes. Turnout was over 77 per cent. The **cantons' majority** was very narrow, however: **11½ to 10½ cantons**. Had a single half-canton voted differently, joining would have failed. **Vaud** said Yes most clearly with 93.2 per cent, while Uri and Schwyz, for example, clearly rejected it.

abschnitte.titel: Neutrality in the League of Nations
abschnitte.text: Switzerland wanted to stay **neutral**. So it was given an exception: it had to take part in **economic sanctions** but not **military** ones. This was called **differential neutrality**. After the sanctions against Italy Switzerland no longer wanted to take part in economic penalties either. In **1938** it was released from this. It returned to comprehensive, **full neutrality**.

abschnitte.titel: Palais des Nations and the end
