abschnitte.text: For the League of Nations a large building was built in Geneva, the **Palais des Nations**. In 1936 the League of Nations moved in there. It could not prevent the **Second World War**, however. In **1946** it was dissolved. The **UN** took over its tasks and uses the Palais des Nations to this day. That is why Geneva is still a city of international organisations.

gewusst: The USA never joined the League of Nations, although its President had suggested it.
Switzerland joined the UN as a full member only in 2002, again after a popular vote.

teile.einleitung: Niklaus von Flüe, known as Brother Klaus, lived in Obwalden in the 15th century. He was a farmer and father of a family and later became a hermit. Many people in Switzerland revere him to this day.
wichtigste: Niklaus von Flüe is called Brother Klaus.
He was born in 1417 in Flüeli near Sachseln in what is now the canton of Obwalden.
With his wife Dorothee he had ten children.
He lived as a hermit in a cell in the Ranft.
It is handed down that he ate nothing for about 19 years.
He was canonised in 1947.
He is regarded as the patron saint of Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: Farmer and father of a family
abschnitte.text: **Niklaus von Flüe** was born in **1417** in **Flüeli** near Sachseln. This is in what is now the canton of **Obwalden**. He was a respected **farmer** and also held offices in his home region, for example as a judge. With his wife **Dorothee Wyss** he had **ten children**. From an early age prayer was very important to him.

abschnitte.titel: The path to becoming a hermit
abschnitte.text: At about 50 years of age Niklaus left his family to live as a **hermit**. A hermit withdraws from other people to live quietly and to **pray**. His wife Dorothee agreed to this. From then on people called him **Brother Klaus**. It was a big step for the whole family.

Brother Klaus lived in a small **cell** in the **Ranft**. This is a gorge near Flüeli, not far from his former home. Beside the cell stands a chapel. It is handed down that he ate nothing for about **19 years**. Many people came to him to ask for advice.

Brother Klaus was known for his wise advice. In 1481 a serious quarrel threatened among the Confederates. At the **Federal Diet in Stans** a priest brought a message from Brother Klaus. Afterwards the states agreed on the **Covenant of Stans**. For this reason Brother Klaus is regarded as a **peacemaker**. He died in 1487.

abschnitte.titel: Saint and patron saint of the country
abschnitte.text: In **1947** Pope **Pius XII** declared Brother Klaus a **saint**. The Catholic Church reveres him as the **patron saint** of Switzerland, that is, as the protector of the country. Many Protestants also respect him. Every year many people make a pilgrimage to Flüeli-Ranft.

gewusst: Brother Klaus lived only a few minutes away from his former farmhouse.
His advice is said to have helped settle a quarrel among the Confederates in 1481.

teile.einleitung: In Swiss history the Restoration is the period from 1814 to 1830. After the fall of Napoleon the old ruling families wanted to restore much of what had applied before the French Revolution. In this period, however, Switzerland also received its present borders and its recognised neutrality.
wichtigste: The Restoration lasted from 1814 to 1830.
From 1815 the Federal Treaty regulated how the cantons lived together.
22 cantons swore to the Federal Treaty of 1815.
Geneva, the Valais and Neuchâtel joined as new cantons in 1815.
On 20 November 1815 the great powers recognised the perpetual neutrality of Switzerland.
The Bernese constitutional lawyer Karl Ludwig von Haller gave the era its name.
In 1816 and 1817 Switzerland suffered severe famine years.

abschnitte.text: **Restoration** means putting something back as it was. After the end of Napoleon's rule, princes and old elites all over Europe wanted the old order back. The term comes from the Bernese constitutional lawyer **Karl Ludwig von Haller**, who wrote a major work entitled “Restoration of the Science of the State”. In Switzerland this period lasted from 1814 to 1830.

From 1815 the **Federal Treaty** regulated how the cantons lived together. It was sworn to by 22 cantons. At that time Switzerland was a loose confederation of states, and the cantons remained almost independent. Common business was handled by the **Federal Diet**, and Zurich, Bern and Lucerne took turns as the leading canton (Vorort).

At the **Congress of Vienna** Europe was reorganised after Napoleon. Geneva, the Valais and Neuchâtel joined the Confederation as new cantons in 1815. Neuchâtel was at the same time a principality of the King of Prussia. Bern received the territory of the former Prince-Bishopric of Basel in the Jura.

On 20 November 1815 the great powers in Paris formally recognised the **perpetual neutrality** of Switzerland. This means that Switzerland does not take part in other states' wars. In 1817 Switzerland joined the **Holy Alliance**, an alliance of monarchs. With the Press and Foreigners Conclusum of 1823 the press was monitored and asylum for refugees was restricted.

In 1815 the volcano **Tambora** erupted in Indonesia and hurled huge amounts of ash into the air. As a result 1816 was very cold and wet in Europe; it is called the year without a summer. There were crop failures, and in Switzerland many people went hungry in 1816 and 1817. It was especially bad in eastern Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: The power of the old elites
abschnitte.text: In cities such as Bern the old families restored the **patriciate**. Under a property-based franchise only men with enough wealth were allowed to vote. The country people had little say. Resistance to this order grew, and from 1830 the Regeneration followed.

begriffe.erklaerung: Putting a former order back in place.
A small group of noble families who ruled a city.
The right to vote only for people with a certain amount of wealth or income.
The canton that led the common business in the old Confederation.
A state does not take part in other states' wars.

gewusst: The famous Lion Monument in Lucerne was unveiled in 1821, in the Restoration period.
Because of the Tambora eruption on the other side of the world, people in Switzerland also went hungry in 1816 and 1817.
Until 1857 Neuchâtel was at the same time a Swiss canton and the possession of the Prussian king.

teile.einleitung: Lousonna was a Roman settlement on the shore of Lake Geneva. The present-day city of Lausanne grew out of it. Its remains lie in the Vidy district, where the International Olympic Committee now has its headquarters.
wichtigste: Lousonna is the Roman predecessor of Lausanne.
It lay in what is now the Vidy district on Lake Geneva.
Lousonna had a harbour on the lakeshore.
At its largest, an estimated 1,500 to 2,000 people lived there.
From the late 3rd century people moved to a protected hill.
Today the IOC headquarters stands in Vidy.

abschnitte.text: **Lousonna** lay on the north shore of **Lake Geneva**, in what is now the Lausanne district of **Vidy**. The settlement was located between the mouths of the rivers Flon and Chamberonne. The name is recorded on old **inscriptions**. The present-day name **Lausanne** developed from it. The Romans called a settlement like this a **vicus**, that is, a village or a small town.

The position on the lake was very good for **trade**. There was a **harbour** on the shore. An inscription by boatmen shows that goods were transported across the water. Boats were often faster in those days than carts on the road. Important roads also ran past Lousonna.

The vicus was about **20 hectares** in size. At its largest, an estimated **1,500 to 2,000** people lived there. This made Lousonna one of the larger settlements in the land of the Helvetii. There were houses, workshops, a marketplace and temples. Parts of the walls can be seen today in a park.

From the late **3rd century** things became unsafe. Germanic groups carried out **raids** into the Roman Empire. So people moved further up to a protected place. There the medieval **bishop's city** of Lausanne with its cathedral later grew up. The old settlement by the lake fell into ruin.

Today Vidy is a district with parks on the lakeshore. In the **Musée romain** of Lausanne-Vidy you can look at finds from Lousonna. Vidy is also home to the **Olympic House**, the headquarters of the **International Olympic Committee**. It stands where parts of the Roman settlement once lay.

gewusst: The name Lausanne goes back to the Roman name Lousonna.
The headquarters of the Olympic movement stands on the site of a Roman settlement.

teile.einleitung: **Chillon Castle** stands on a rock in **Lake Geneva** near Montreux. It is one of the best-known castles in Switzerland. For many centuries it was an important fortress; today it is a museum.
wichtigste: Chillon Castle stands on a rocky islet in Lake Geneva.
It belongs to the municipality of Veytaux in the canton of Vaud.
The Counts of Savoy expanded it into a large fortress.
François Bonivard was held prisoner in the dungeon for several years.
In 1536 the Bernese conquered the castle.
In 1816 Lord Byron wrote the poem “The Prisoner of Chillon”.
Today Chillon is a museum.

abschnitte.text: Chillon Castle stands on a small **rocky islet** in **Lake Geneva**. This way it was surrounded by water and well protected. It lies in the municipality of **Veytaux** near **Montreux** in the **canton of Vaud**. Between the lake and the steep mountains an important **road** ran past here, the link to Italy over the Great St Bernard.

In the Middle Ages the **Counts of Savoy** expanded Chillon into a large fortress. From here they **controlled** the road along the lake and charged **tolls**. The castle also served as a residence and as a **prison**. The walls, towers and halls from this period can still be seen today.

The best-known prisoner was **François Bonivard**. He was a monk from Geneva who had turned against the **Duke of Savoy**. So he sat for several years in the **dungeon** of Chillon, chained to a pillar. In **1536** the **Bernese** conquered Vaud and Chillon too. In doing so they freed Bonivard. After that the castle belonged to Bern for a long time.

The English poet **Lord Byron** visited Chillon in **1816**. He wrote the poem **“The Prisoner of Chillon”** about Bonivard. The poem made the castle famous all over Europe. In the dungeon the name **“Byron”** is carved into a pillar. People say he carved it himself. This is not certain, however.

Today Chillon Castle is a **museum** and belongs to the **canton of Vaud**. You can walk through halls, courtyards, towers and the dungeons in the rock. Every year very many visitors come from all over the world.

gewusst: Chillon Castle is one of the most visited historic buildings in Switzerland.
Chillon has belonged to the canton of Vaud since 1803, that is, since this canton has existed.

teile.einleitung: With a popular initiative citizens in Switzerland can demand a change to the Federal Constitution. For this they have to collect enough signatures. After that the people and the cantons vote on it.
wichtigste: A popular initiative demands a change to the Federal Constitution.
Since 1848 one could demand a total revision of the Constitution.
In 1891 the initiative for individual articles was introduced, with 50,000 signatures.
Since 1977 it has needed 100,000 signatures.
There are 18 months to collect them (as of 2025).
It is accepted only with a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.
The first accepted initiative, in 1893, was the ban on kosher slaughter.

abschnitte.text: The Federal Constitution of **1848** already allowed **50,000** eligible voters to demand a **total revision**. That means the whole Constitution was to be reworked. Individual new articles could not be proposed in this way, however. This form was hardly used. In **1891** the initiative for a **partial revision** was added. Now one could change or add to a single article in a targeted way. For this too 50,000 signatures were needed.

A group of people forms an **initiative committee**. It writes a text for the new constitutional provision. From publication in the **Federal Gazette** a period of **18 months** runs (as of 2025). In this time enough valid **signatures** are needed. Because the population grew and women received the vote in 1971, the number was doubled to **100,000** in **1977**. If enough signatures come together, the initiative has succeeded.

The Federal Council and Parliament then discuss the initiative. They can give a recommendation. If they find the aim partly good, they can draw up a **counter-proposal**. Often the initiative is then withdrawn. At the end the eligible voters vote. Because the Constitution changes, the **majority of the people** and the **majority of the cantons** are needed. That means the majority of those voting and the majority of the cantons must agree.

On **20 August 1893** a popular initiative was accepted by the people and the cantons for the first time. It demanded a **ban on kosher slaughter** (Schächten). That means animals must be stunned before slaughter. The initiative was justified with **animal welfare**. But it was also directed against the **Jewish minority**, whose religious rules require this form of slaughter. Since then the people and the cantons have voted on many hundreds of initiatives, most of which were rejected.

gewusst: The popular initiative also exists in the cantons and often in the municipalities.
Only a small part of all popular initiatives is accepted at the ballot box.

teile.einleitung: The **Priests' Charter** (Pfaffenbrief) was an agreement between several Confederate states in 1370. It mainly regulated which court clergy had to go before, and it kept the peace on the road to the Gotthard.
wichtigste: The Priests' Charter was agreed on 7 October 1370.
“Pfaffen” was an old word for clergy.
In secular disputes, clergy had to go before the court of the state.
For marriage and Church matters, the Church court remained responsible.
Zurich, Lucerne, Zug, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden made the charter; Bern and Glarus did not.
The trigger was an attack by the Zurich provost Bruno Brun.

abschnitte.text: The word **Pfaffe** used to mean simply a priest or **clergyman**. Today it sounds disparaging, but then it was an ordinary expression. In the Middle Ages clergy had many privileges. In disputes they could often go before **Church** or foreign courts and so avoid the courts of the city.

The trigger was an incident in 1370. **Bruno Brun**, provost of the Grossmünster in Zurich, attacked the mayor (Schultheiss) of Lucerne and held him prisoner. He would not recognise a secular court. Zurich then **banished** him from the city. Brun asked Austria for help.

On **7 October 1370** **Zurich, Lucerne, Zug, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden** made the Priests' Charter. **Bern** and **Glarus** did not take part. In secular disputes clergy were no longer allowed to appeal to foreign courts but were subject to the **local courts**. Only in **marriage and spiritual matters** did the Church remain responsible. Austrian servants in the territory of the states also had to swear an **oath to the Confederates**.

abschnitte.titel: A safe road to the Gotthard
abschnitte.text: The states also promised peace on the **road from Zurich to the Gotthard**. Nobody was to attack travellers or merchants on this route. Safe roads were very important for trade. Anyone who broke the order was to be punished.

abschnitte.titel: From personal law to territorial law
abschnitte.text: Research sees in the Priests' Charter a change in legal thinking. Earlier, the **status of a person** often decided which court was responsible. Now what counted was the **territory** in which someone lived. In this way the states asserted their rule over their own territory.

gewusst: In the Priests' Charter the word “Eidgenossenschaft” (Confederation) appears for the first time in a document.
Bruno Brun was a son of the first mayor of Zurich, Rudolf Brun.

teile.einleitung: Thomas Platter the Elder lived in the 16th century. He grew up as a poor goatherd in Valais and later became a learned headmaster and printer in Basel. His life story is still known today.
wichtigste: Thomas Platter was born in 1499 in Grächen in Valais.
As a small boy he herded goats.
As a teenager he wandered about as a travelling scholar.
In Zurich he learned the trade of rope maker.
In Basel he ran a Latin school and operated a printing works.
His son Felix became a famous doctor.
Thomas Platter died in 1582 in Basel.

abschnitte.text: Thomas Platter was born in **1499** in **Grächen** in Valais. His family was very poor. Even as a small child he had to herd **goats**. Life in the mountains was hard and often dangerous. Later he described exactly how as a child he had gone hungry and frozen.

As a teenager Platter wandered as a **travelling scholar** through foreign lands. Such pupils went from town to town to attend a school. To survive they sang and begged. At first Platter learned little in this way. Only as a young man did he begin to study hard.

In **Zurich** Platter learned the trade of **rope maker**, that is, how to twist ropes. On the side he learned old languages such as **Latin**, **Greek** and Hebrew. He was a follower of the **Reformation**. Later he moved to **Basel**. There for many years he led the Latin school at Burg. Alongside this he ran a **printing works** with others. One of the books that appeared there was an important work by the reformer Calvin.

In old age Thomas Platter wrote down his **life story** for his son **Felix**. In it he tells openly of poverty, hunger and his laborious road to education. That is why we know a great deal today about the life of a poor child in those times. His son Felix Platter became a famous **doctor** in Basel. Thomas Platter died in **1582** in Basel.

gewusst: As an adult Platter learned Hebrew so well that he could teach the language himself.
His life story is regarded as one of the most important self-portraits from the time of the Reformation.

teile.einleitung: The Devil's Bridge crosses the Reuss in the canton of Uri in the wild Schöllenen Gorge. It lies on the way to the Gotthard Pass. A famous legend surrounds its building.
wichtigste: The Devil's Bridge stands in the Schöllenen Gorge in the canton of Uri.
Below the bridge flows the Reuss.
The way leads to Andermatt and on to the Gotthard.
According to the legend the Devil built the bridge.
The people of Uri sent a billy goat across first.
In 1799 the Russian General Suvorov fought here.

abschnitte.text: The **Schöllenen** is a very narrow and steep gorge in the canton of **Uri**. Through it the **Reuss** rushes northwards. For a long time the gorge was a great obstacle on the way south. Only with a bridge could it be crossed easily. The Devil's Bridge joins Göschenen with **Andermatt**. From there the way goes on over the **Gotthard Pass** to Italy.

According to the legend the people of Uri could not manage to build a bridge over the gorge. Then the **Devil** offered his help. As his reward he wanted the **soul** of whoever first crossed the bridge. The people of Uri agreed to the deal. But they were clever: they sent a **billy goat** across the bridge first. So the Devil got no human being.

The Devil grew very angry about this. He fetched a huge rock to destroy the bridge. But he missed his target, and the bridge stayed standing. The rock is called the **Devil's Stone** and lies near **Göschenen**. When the motorway was built in the 1970s, the big stone was moved a little.

In **1799** Russian troops under General **Suvorov** fought the French in the Schöllenen. A monument in the rock recalls the fallen soldiers. The bridge was rebuilt several times over the years. The present stone bridge dates from the 19th century. Above it runs a newer road bridge for cars.

gewusst: A big devil is painted on the rock face beside the bridge.
The Suvorov monument is a huge cross cut straight into the rock face.

tcik6cu.t: Proportional election of the National Council

teile.einleitung: Since 1919 the National Council has been elected by **proportional representation**. This means that the parties get as many seats as correspond to their share of the votes. Its introduction greatly changed Swiss politics.
wichtigste: Until 1919 the National Council was elected by majority vote.
Under proportional representation, parties get seats according to their share of the votes.
On 13 October 1918 the people accepted the proportional representation initiative.
It was the third attempt after 1900 and 1910.
The first proportional election took place on 26 October 1919.
The Liberals lost their absolute majority.

abschnitte.text: With a **majority vote** the person with the most votes wins. Smaller parties often come away empty-handed. From 1848 this above all benefited the **Liberal Party**. With **proportional representation**, seats are shared out according to the share of the votes. This means smaller parties also get into parliament.

Popular initiatives for proportional representation failed in **1900** and **1910**. Only the **third attempt** succeeded. On **13 October 1918** the people accepted the initiative with about **two thirds in favour**. The majority of the cantons, the **cantonal majority**, was also clearly reached. Shortly afterwards, in November 1918, came the General Strike, in which proportional representation was also an important demand.

On **26 October 1919** the National Council was elected by proportional representation for the first time. About **80 per cent** of those entitled to vote went to the polls, as many as never since. The **Liberals** lost over 40 seats and with them their **absolute majority**. The **Social Democrats** almost doubled their seats. The **Farmers' and Citizens' parties** entered as a new force with about 30 seats.

Since 1919 no party has been able to govern alone. The parties have to work together and find compromises. The Farmers' and Citizens' parties later gave rise to the **SVP** (Swiss People's Party). By the way, the **Council of States** is still elected by majority vote in most cantons.

gewusst: The turnout of about 80 per cent in 1919 is still the highest for a National Council election.
Since 1919 no party has achieved an absolute majority in the National Council on its own.

teile.einleitung: Louis Favre was a building contractor from the Geneva area. He led the construction of the Gotthard railway tunnel, one of the greatest building projects of his time. However, he did not live to see it finished.
wichtigste: Louis Favre was a building contractor.
He came from Chêne-Bourg near Geneva.
He led the construction of the Gotthard Tunnel.
In July 1879 he died during an inspection in the tunnel.
On 29 February 1880 the two teams of builders met inside the mountain.
Favre did not live to see the breakthrough.

abschnitte.text: **Louis Favre** came from **Chêne-Bourg** near Geneva. He was a **building contractor**, that is, someone who plans large construction work and carries it out with his workers. Before the Gotthard he had already built other tunnels. In 1872 he won the contract for the great tunnel at the Gotthard. He promised to finish the work in a short time.

The **Gotthard Tunnel** was to carry the railway from Göschenen in the canton of Uri to Airolo in Ticino. It is about 15 kilometres long. Work went on from both sides at the same time. The workers used **explosives** and drilling machines driven by compressed air. Many workers came from Italy. The work was hard and dangerous, and many workers lost their lives.

In July **1879** Louis Favre carried out an inspection in the tunnel. He suddenly felt unwell. Shortly afterwards he died of **heart failure**. The tunnel was not yet finished, and he did not live to see the end.

On **29 February 1880** the workers from the north and the south met inside the mountain. This moment is called the **breakthrough**. The two tunnels met each other very precisely. In 1882 the Gotthard Railway was opened. For the first time you could now travel by train under the Alps to the south.

gewusst: The breakthrough at the Gotthard took place on 29 February, in a leap year.
Louis Favre died in the tunnel he had built, only a few months before the breakthrough.

teile.einleitung: The Schöllenen is a wild, narrow gorge of the River Reuss in the canton of Uri. It lies between Göschenen and Andermatt on the way to the Gotthard Pass. Anyone who wanted to get through it needed bold bridges and later a tunnel through the rock.
wichtigste: The Schöllenen is a gorge of the Reuss between Göschenen and Andermatt.
Around 1200 Walser settlers from the Urseren valley probably made the gorge passable with a pack-animal track.
In 1707 and 1708 Pietro Morettini built the Urnerloch, the first road tunnel in Switzerland.
The stone Devil's Bridge of 1595 collapsed in 1888.
The present third Devil's Bridge for cars was opened in 1958.

abschnitte.text: In the **Schöllenen** the **Reuss** squeezes through steep rock walls. For a long time the gorge was a great obstacle on the way over the **Gotthard**. It is assumed that around 1200 **Walser** settlers from the Urseren valley laid out a **pack-animal track** with bridges over the Reuss. A pack-animal track is a narrow path for beasts of burden. This is not firmly documented, however, and the exact date of construction is disputed.

In the past you had to get round a rock face on a hanging walkway, the **Twärrenbrücke**. In 1707 and 1708 the Ticinese master builder **Pietro Morettini** blasted a passage through the rock. Morettini was a pupil of the famous French fortress builder Vauban. The tunnel was originally 64 metres long and is called the **Urnerloch**. It is regarded as the first **road tunnel** in Switzerland. The construction turned out considerably more expensive than planned.

The famous **Devil's Bridge** crosses the Reuss. In 1595 a stone bridge was built. In 1830 a new bridge was opened beside it, and the old one was no longer maintained. On 2 August 1888 it collapsed. In 1958 a third, wider bridge for **motor traffic** was added. The 19th-century bridge is now used by pedestrians and cyclists.

A well-known **legend** is woven around the Devil's Bridge. The people of Uri could not manage to build a bridge over the gorge. The Devil offered to build it. As his reward he wanted the soul of the first to cross it. The clever people of Uri sent a billy goat across first. A large figure of the Devil on the rock face recalls the legend.

gewusst: The Urnerloch is regarded as the oldest road tunnel in Switzerland.
Today two bridges from different centuries stand side by side at the Devil's Bridge.

tf8jc42.t: Battle of St Jakob an der Birs

teile.einleitung: On 26 August 1444 a small band of Confederates fought at **St Jakob an der Birs** outside Basel against a huge French army. Almost all the Confederates fell. Even so, the French army withdrew afterwards.
wichtigste: The battle took place on 26 August 1444, during the Old Zurich War.
St Jakob lies on the Birs on the edge of Basel.
The French army of the Armagnacs was led by the Dauphin Louis.
About 1,500 Confederates faced an army many times larger.
Almost all the Confederates fell.
In October 1444 the Dauphin and the Confederates made the Peace of Ensisheim.

abschnitte.text: In the **Old Zurich War** the Confederates fought against **Zurich**, which had allied itself with the **Habsburgs**. Zurich and the Habsburgs asked the King of France for help. A large mercenary army, the **Armagnacs**, then marched against the Confederates. It was led by the **Dauphin Louis**, the heir to the French throne. He later became King **Louis XI**.

At that time the Confederates were besieging the **Farnsburg** in the Baselbiet. A detachment of about **1,500 men** marched from there against the Armagnacs. It had orders not to advance further. But the men crossed the **Birs** **against orders** and attacked the huge army. It is said to have numbered about 20,000 men.

The small band was far inferior to the enemy. The last Confederates withdrew into the walled **garden of the Siechenhaus**. A Siechenhaus was a house for the sick outside the town. There they were overcome after fierce fighting. **Almost all the Confederates fell**.

The Armagnacs, too, had **very heavy losses**. The Dauphin noticed how hard the Confederates fought. He gave up on an attack on the Confederation. In October 1444 he made the **Peace of Ensisheim** in Alsace with them. After that the Armagnacs withdrew.

Today a **monument**, the **St Jakob Monument**, stands near the battlefield. Nearby lies the football stadium **St. Jakob-Park**. Until the 19th century a red wine called **“Schweizerblut”** (“Swiss blood”) was grown there. The name recalled the fallen Confederates.

gewusst: The St Jakob Monument in Basel was unveiled in 1872.
The battle was later often compared with the Spartans at Thermopylae.

teile.einleitung: Today many people come to Switzerland. In the past it was often the other way round: many Swiss emigrated because they had no work at home or too little to eat. Especially in the 19th century they looked overseas for a new life.
wichtigste: In the 19th century many Swiss emigrated because of poverty and hunger.
The most emigrants overseas were from 1881 to 1890, over 90,000 people.
Towards the end of the 19th century almost 90 per cent went to North America.
People from Fribourg founded Nova Friburgo in Brazil in 1819, people from Glarus founded New Glarus in Wisconsin in 1845.
A federal law of 1880 placed the emigration agencies under supervision.
Around 1900 most Swiss living abroad in Europe lived in France.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century Switzerland was still a poor country. Crop failures, years of famine and an **agricultural crisis** made life hard. Many families had too little land to live from. At the same time, boat fares across the Atlantic became cheaper. So many decided to start again in a distant country.

Towards the end of the 19th century almost 90 per cent of overseas emigrants chose **North America**. The USA attracted them with land and work. In the decade from **1881 to 1890** over 90,000 people left Switzerland for overseas, more than ever before in a decade. South America and other continents played a smaller role in numbers.

Some emigrants founded settlements of their own. In 1819 **Nova Friburgo** was founded in the hills of **Brazil** near Rio de Janeiro by families from the canton of Fribourg. In 1845 emigrants from Glarus founded the settlement of **New Glarus** in the US state of **Wisconsin**. The Glarus government at that time supported the emigration of poor families. New Glarus keeps up Swiss traditions to this day.

In the past the **home municipality** had to look after its poor citizens. So some municipalities paid for poor families' passage to America. In this way they wanted to save future **poor relief**. Often the emigrants had to give up their **citizenship** in return. For those affected it was a farewell for ever.

Many emigrants travelled with the help of **emigration agencies**. Some agencies deceived and cheated their customers. Based on the Federal Constitution of 1874, the federal government therefore passed a law in 1880. It placed the agencies under state supervision. Not everyone went overseas, by the way: around 1900 about 87,000 Swiss lived in neighbouring **France**.

gewusst: The settlement of Nova Friburgo in Brazil still bears the name of its founders' homeland to this day.
Many Swiss people also live abroad today; they are called Swiss abroad (Auslandschweizer).

teile.einleitung: Vindonissa was a large Roman legionary camp in present day Windisch in the canton of Aargau. In the 1st century AD thousands of soldiers lived here. Finds from Vindonissa tell a great deal about their daily life.
wichtigste: Vindonissa lay where the Aare, Reuss and Limmat meet.
Around AD 14 the 13th Legion built a first camp of wood.
The 21st Legion extended the camp in stone.
In the rubbish mound about 600 wooden writing tablets were found.
Around AD 300 the Castrum Vindonissense arose.
Around 600 the bishop's seat was moved to Constance.

abschnitte.text: Vindonissa lay in present day **Windisch** in Aargau on a plateau. Nearby, at the **Wasserschloss**, the **Reuss** and the **Limmat** flow into the **Aare**. From here the Romans could control important routes and rivers. So they built a **legionary camp** here. A legion was a large force of several thousand soldiers.

Around **AD 14** the **Legio XIII Gemina**, the 13th Legion, set up a first camp of wood. It stayed for about three decades. From about AD 45 to 69 the **Legio XXI Rapax** was stationed here. “Rapax” means “the grasping one”. It extended the camp in **stone**. In the year 69, the **Year of the Four Emperors**, it marched to Italy with Vitellius. After that a further legion came to Vindonissa.

At the **north gate** the soldiers threw their rubbish onto a big mound. This **rubbish mound** is today a treasure for research. In the damp ground leather, wood and other materials were preserved. About **600 writing tablets** of wood were found. They were coated with **wax**, in which one wrote with a **stylus**. Where the stylus pressed through to the wood, the writing is still legible today.

Around **AD 300** a new fort arose on the site, the **Castrum Vindonissense**. It belonged to a frontier defence along the Danube, Iller and Rhine. After 406 it was abandoned. In the 6th century a **bishop** of Windisch is attested, **Bubulcus**. Around 600 the bishop's seat was moved to **Constance** on Lake Constance.

gewusst: In Windisch remains of a Roman amphitheatre are preserved, which had room for thousands of spectators.
The writing tablets from Vindonissa contain letters, accounts and addresses of soldiers.

teile.einleitung: Matthäus Merian the Elder was a copper engraver and publisher from Basel. He drew hundreds of views of towns and cities. His pictures show us today what towns looked like almost 400 years ago.
wichtigste: Matthäus Merian was born in Basel in 1593.
He made his pictures as copper engravings.
He especially liked drawing views of towns and cities.
In 1615 he drew Basel from a bird's-eye view.
In Frankfurt he ran a publishing house.
His “Topographia” shows countries and towns.
His daughter Maria Sibylla became famous for her pictures of butterflies.

abschnitte.text: **Matthäus Merian** was born in **Basel** in **1593**. He learned the craft of **copper engraving**. Afterwards he travelled through various countries and worked in several towns. Later he settled in **Frankfurt**. There he spent most of his life.

In **copper engraving** you scratch a picture, in mirror image, into a smooth **copper plate**. Then you rub ink into the grooves. With a press you print the picture on paper. Many **prints** can be made from one plate. So Merian's pictures could be sold in large numbers.

In **1615** Merian drew a famous plan of Basel. It shows the city from a **bird's-eye view**, that is, as if you were flying over it like a bird. You can see all the houses, lanes, churches and the Rhine. The plan is very precise. It is an important record of old Basel.

Merian married into a **Frankfurt publishing family**. Soon he was running a **publishing house** himself. His greatest work is the **“Topographia”**. It is a large series of books with pictures and descriptions of towns and regions. There is also a volume on **Switzerland**. The texts were mostly written by the scholar Martin Zeiller.

Merian's daughter **Maria Sibylla Merian** became famous herself. She painted **caterpillars and butterflies** very precisely and even travelled to South America for this. Two sons also worked as artists. Many old houses and walls no longer exist today. On Merian's pictures you can still see them, so they are very **valuable** for history.

gewusst: Merian's pictures show towns as they looked in the 17th century.
His daughter Maria Sibylla Merian travelled to South America around 1700 to study butterflies.

teile.einleitung: Swiss wrestling, or Schwingen, is a Swiss form of wrestling. Two wrestlers fight in sawdust and try to put their opponent on his back. The sport is among the best known traditions of Switzerland.
wichtigste: Schwingen is a Swiss way of wrestling.
The fighting takes place on a round ring of sawdust.
The wrestlers grip each other by the short wrestling trousers.
The winner is the one who brings the opponent to the ground with both shoulder blades.
The Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival takes place every three years.
The winner is called Schwingerkönig (king of the wrestlers) and receives a bull, the Siegermuni.

abschnitte.text: In Schwingen two wrestlers fight each other. One bout is called a **Gang**. Both try to throw the opponent on his back with a **swing**. The winner is the one who brings the opponent to the ground with both **shoulder blades**. Then the bout is decided.

The wrestlers fight on a round ring of **sawdust**. The soft sawdust protects them when they fall. Over their clothes they wear short **wrestling trousers** made of strong cloth. The opponent grips them by these trousers. Without them Schwingen would not be possible at all.

Fairness is very important in Schwingen. After the bout the two shake hands. The winner brushes the **sawdust off the loser's back**. That is a sign of respect. So wrestlers remain good friends even after a hard fight.

The biggest festival is the **Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival**. It takes place **every three years** and is one of the biggest sporting festivals in Switzerland. Whoever wins it becomes **Schwingerkönig**. That is the highest title in Schwingen. The best wrestlers also receive a **wreath**.

The Schwingerkönig does not get a gold trophy but a young bull. It is called the **Siegermuni**. “Muni” is the Swiss word for bull. Besides the Muni there is a big **prize pavilion** at the festival with many more prizes.

gewusst: “Muni” is the Swiss German word for bull.
The wrestling trousers are made of strong cloth so that the opponent can pull hard on them.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has been a member of the United Nations, the UN for short, since 10 September 2002. The road there was long, because the people at first clearly rejected membership in 1986. Only in 2002 did the people and the cantons narrowly say yes.
wichtigste: On 16 March 1986 the people rejected UN membership with about 75 per cent No and without a single canton.
On 3 March 2002 the people and the cantons agreed to membership.
The Yes share in 2002 was about 54.6 per cent, and the cantons' majority was very narrow at 12 to 11.
Switzerland is the only country to have joined the UN following a popular vote.
On 10 September 2002 it was admitted as the 190th member.
Before that Switzerland had had observer status since 1948.
In 2023 and 2024 Switzerland was for the first time a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council.

abschnitte.text: The **United Nations**, UN for short, was founded in 1945 after the Second World War. Almost all the states of the world are members. The UN works for peace, human rights and cooperation. Geneva is the European headquarters of the UN; the main headquarters is in New York.

abschnitte.titel: For a long time only an observer
abschnitte.text: As early as 1920 Switzerland had joined the **League of Nations**, the forerunner of the UN. At first it stayed outside the UN because it feared for its **neutrality**. From 1948, however, it had observer status. It also worked in many UN organisations without being a full member.

On 16 March 1986 the people voted on membership for the first time. About 75 per cent said No, and not a single canton agreed. The opponents were worried above all about Switzerland's neutrality. Many feared that otherwise Switzerland would have to take part in the conflicts of other countries.

A **popular initiative** brought the subject to the ballot box again. On 3 March 2002 about 54.6 per cent of those voting said Yes. The **cantons' majority** was extremely narrow, at 12 to 11 cantonal votes. With that Switzerland became the only country in the world to join the UN following a popular vote.

On 10 September 2002 Switzerland was admitted in New York as the 190th member. Shortly afterwards East Timor joined as the 191st member. In 2023 and 2024 Switzerland sat for the first time as a non-permanent member on the **Security Council**. There important decisions on peace and security are taken.

In Geneva stands the **Palais des Nations**, which formerly belonged to the League of Nations. Today thousands of people work there and in many other organisations. In Geneva sit, for example, the World Health Organization and the High Commissioner for Refugees. That is why Switzerland plays an important role in international cooperation.

begriffe.erklaerung: United Nations, an organisation of almost all the states of the world for peace and cooperation.
You may be present at meetings but not vote.
A majority of the cantons in a vote.
The most important UN body for peace, with 5 permanent and 10 changing members.

gewusst: In front of the Palais des Nations in Geneva stands a huge chair with a broken leg, which recalls the victims of landmines.
Switzerland was host to the UN in Geneva for a long time before it became a member itself.

teile.einleitung: The watch industry is one of the best known branches of the Swiss economy. It began in Geneva and spread across the Jura. Its history tells of the Reformation, home work and great upheavals.
wichtigste: From 1541 Calvin banned jewellery in Geneva, so many goldsmiths became watchmakers.
In 1601 a watchmakers' guild arose in Geneva.
In the Jura watchmaking was a sideline for farmers in winter.
In the Établissage many workshops each made individual parts.
In 1876 the World's Fair in Philadelphia showed American mass production.
La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle have been UNESCO World Heritage since 2009.

abschnitte.text: In 1541 the reformer **John Calvin** enforced strict rules in Geneva. The wearing of **jewellery** and finery was forbidden. Many **goldsmiths** and jewellers lost their work in this way. They turned to the making of **watches**, which were regarded as useful. In 1601 the Geneva watchmakers founded a **guild** of their own. It regulated training, quality and who might practise the trade.

abschnitte.titel: Farmers as watchmakers in the Jura
abschnitte.text: In the 18th century watchmaking spread in the **Jura**. The soil there was poor and the winters long. The farming families needed an additional income. Watch parts needed little raw material but were worth a lot. So watchmaking became an ideal **sideline**. According to a legend the goldsmith **Daniel JeanRichard** from La Sagne is said to have founded watchmaking in the Neuchâtel Jura. Historians today regard his role as sole founder as exaggerated.

Typical of the Jura was the **Établissage**. In it wheels, springs or cases were made in many small, separate workshops, often in farmhouses. An entrepreneur, the **Établisseur**, bought the parts in. He had them assembled into the finished watch and sold it. So many people worked on a single watch, each on his own part.

At the **World's Fair of 1876 in Philadelphia** Swiss watchmakers saw something threatening. American factories made watches with machines in large numbers, with **interchangeable parts**. After that the Swiss watch industry modernised, and **factories** arose. The towns of **La Chaux-de-Fonds** and **Le Locle** were planned entirely for the watchmakers. Since 2009 they have been **UNESCO World Heritage** as the “Watchmaking Town Planning”.

gewusst: In La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle the streets and houses are laid out so that a lot of light falls on the workbenches.
In the 1970s the Swiss watch industry fell into a severe crisis because of cheap quartz watches from Asia.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Federal Railways, SBB for short, are the biggest railway company in Switzerland. They came into being in 1902, when the federal government took over the large private railways. They still belong to the federal government today.
wichtigste: The SBB began operating on 1 January 1902.
In 1898 the people voted to buy back the large private railways.
Five large private railways merged into the SBB, the Gotthard Railway being the last, in 1909.
The SBB head office is in Bern.
After the First World War the lines were electrified because of a shortage of coal.
Since 1999 the SBB have been a joint-stock company owned by the federal government.

abschnitte.titel: From private railways to a state network
abschnitte.text: In the 19th century **private companies** built the Swiss railways. They often competed with each other. In 1898 the people voted on the **buying back** of the large private railways by the federal government. Under the motto “The Swiss railways for the Swiss people” they clearly accepted the law. On 1 January 1902 the **SBB** began operating.

Five large private railways merged into the SBB: the **Central Railway**, the **North Eastern Railway**, the **United Swiss Railways**, the **Jura-Simplon Railway** and the **Gotthard Railway**. The Gotthard Railway came last, only in 1909. Because of treaties with Germany and Italy its takeover took longer. These countries had helped to pay for the building of the Gotthard Railway.

In 1906 the **Simplon Tunnel** was opened. It links Brig in Valais with Domodossola in Italy. At the time it was the longest railway tunnel in the world. The SBB operated it from the start. Later further large tunnels followed, for example the **Gotthard Base Tunnel** in 2016.

Steam locomotives needed **coal**, and Switzerland had to import it. In the First World War coal became scarce. So after the war the SBB began to **electrify** their lines. The electricity came from the **water power** of the mountains. That made the country less dependent on imports.

The head office of the SBB is in the federal city of **Bern**. Since 1999 the SBB have been a **joint-stock company** under special law. All the shares belong to the Confederation. The SBB carry passengers and goods and are among the most important companies in Switzerland.

gewusst: When it opened in 1906 the Simplon Tunnel was the longest railway tunnel in the world.
A large part of the electricity for the SBB comes from water power.

teile.einleitung: The Vitznau Rigi Railway runs from Vitznau on Lake Lucerne up the Rigi. It was opened in 1871 and was the first mountain railway in Europe. Because the mountain is so steep, it runs on a cogwheel.
wichtigste: The railway runs from Vitznau up the Rigi.
It was opened on 21 May 1871.
It was the first mountain railway in Europe.
It was built by the engineer Niklaus Riggenbach.
The Rigi stands between Lake Lucerne and Lake Zug.
On a rack railway a cogwheel engages in a rack.

abschnitte.text: The **Rigi** stands between **Lake Lucerne** and **Lake Zug**. From the top there is a wide view over lakes and Alps. So many tourists wanted to go up early on. For a long time that was possible only on foot, on horses or in carrying chairs. The railway was meant to make the ascent much more comfortable.

An ordinary train slips on a steep slope. On a **rack railway** there is therefore a **rack** between the rails. The locomotive has a **cogwheel** that engages in this rack. In this way the train can travel up steep mountains and safely down again. The engineer **Niklaus Riggenbach** had invented this system with a rack.

abschnitte.titel: The first mountain railway in Europe
abschnitte.text: On **21 May 1871** the railway was opened from **Vitznau**. It was the **first mountain railway in Europe**. At the start it ran with **steam locomotives**. Today the trains mostly run on electricity. For special trips, though, old steam locomotives are still used. A few years later a railway up the Rigi from Arth-Goldau was added too.

gewusst: The Rigi is often called the “Queen of the Mountains”.
Riggenbach's rack system was later used for many other mountain railways too.

teile.einleitung: The Opera House Riot of May 1980 was the beginning of the Zurich youth unrest. Young people demanded space for their own culture. The events are known as the Eighties Movement.
wichtigste: The trigger was a loan of 60 million francs for the opera house.
The riot began on the evening of 30 May 1980.
People coming from a Bob Marley concert joined the demonstration.
The movement demanded an Autonomous Youth Centre (AJZ).
A well-known slogan was “We want everything, and we want it subito!”.
The film “Züri brännt” shows the events from the movement's point of view.
The AJZ was near the main station and was demolished in 1982.

abschnitte.text: In 1980 the city of Zurich approved **60 million francs** for the renovation of the **opera house**. Many young people were angry about this. They felt that nothing was being done for their own culture. There were no places for concerts, theatre and meetings. The loan became a symbol of this injustice.

On the evening of **30 May 1980** young people gathered in front of the opera house. During the night there were **riots** with the police. On the same evening **Bob Marley** gave a concert in the Hallenstadion. People from the concert joined the demonstration, and the crowd grew greatly. This evening is seen as the starting point of the **Eighties Movement**.

Above all the movement demanded an **Autonomous Youth Centre**, or **AJZ** for short. Autonomous means self-managed. The young people wanted to decide for themselves what happened there. In 1980 the AJZ was opened in a building near the **main station**. It was closed several times and was demolished in **1982**.

The movement was impatient with the authorities and with society. This is shown by its best-known slogan: **“We want everything, and we want it subito!”**. Subito is Italian and means immediately. The **Videoladen Zürich** made the documentary film **“Züri brännt”** (“Zurich is burning”). It came out in 1981 and shows the events from the movement's point of view.

There was heated argument over the unrest. Some saw in the movement a justified call for free spaces. Others condemned the **violence** and the damage to property. Similar movements also appeared in other Swiss cities such as **Bern**, **Basel** and **Lausanne**. The discussion about spaces for youth culture has changed the cities in the long term.

gewusst: A Bob Marley concert happened to play a part in the start of the unrest.
The slogan “Wir wollen alles, und zwar subito!” mixes German and Italian.

teile.einleitung: In 1332 the city of Lucerne made an alliance with Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden. At that time Lucerne was under Habsburg rule. The alliance led to tensions and finally to the Sempach War.
wichtigste: In 1332 Lucerne allied itself with Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden.
The alliance expressly reserved the rights of the Habsburgs.
In Lucerne there were tensions between friends of the alliance and circles loyal to the Habsburgs.
In 1385 the people of Lucerne destroyed the Habsburg castle of Rothenburg.
In 1386 the Confederates defeated Duke Leopold III at Sempach.
The Lucerne mayor Petermann von Gundoldingen fell in the battle.

abschnitte.text: In **1332** **Lucerne** made an alliance with the three forest cantons **Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden**. At that time the city belonged to the **Habsburgs**. So the Habsburgs' rights as rulers were expressly **reserved** in the alliance. On paper, everything stayed as it was. In practice, though, the alliance weakened the Habsburgs' position in Lucerne.

Not everyone in Lucerne was in favour of the alliance. Part of the nobility and of the townspeople continued to side with the **rule of Austria**, that is, with the Habsburgs. Others wanted to work more closely with the forest cantons. For decades Lucerne was therefore torn between **two camps**. There were quarrels again and again.

North of the city the Habsburgs owned **Rothenburg** castle with a toll station. Anyone who brought goods past it had to pay **toll**. The people of Lucerne were very annoyed by this. In 1385 they destroyed the castle. This was an open challenge to the Habsburgs and helped to bring about the **Sempach War**.

In **1386** the **Battle of Sempach** took place. The Confederates defeated the army of **Duke Leopold III** of Austria. The duke fell in the fighting. The Lucerne **mayor Petermann von Gundoldingen** also died in the battle. He had led the people of Lucerne and was one of their most important politicians.

After the victory at Sempach, Lucerne was finally free of **Habsburg rule**. The city could now expand its territory greatly. It acquired many villages and districts in the surrounding area. Over time the present-day **canton of Lucerne** grew out of this.

gewusst: Lucerne was the first city to ally with the forest cantons.
At Sempach both leaders fell: Duke Leopold III and the Lucerne mayor Gundoldingen.

teile.einleitung: The Milan Wars were a series of wars over the rich Duchy of Milan around 1500. The Confederates fought in them as mercenaries and on their own account. In the end they lost at Marignano, but gained the area of present-day Ticino.
wichtigste: The Milan Wars were about the Duchy of Milan.
In 1500 Bellinzona passed to Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden.
In the Pavia Expedition of 1512 the Confederates drove the French out of Milan.
In 1513 the Confederates won at Novara.
In 1515 King Francis I of France defeated the Confederates at Marignano.
Cardinal Matthäus Schiner was an important opponent of France.
The Confederates gained the area of present-day Ticino.

abschnitte.text: Around 1500 the **Duchy of Milan** was one of the richest areas in Europe. France, the Habsburgs, Venice, the Pope and the Confederates all wanted influence there. The Confederates often fought as **mercenaries**, that is, for foreign lords in return for pay. Sometimes, though, they also fought on their own account. Swiss foot soldiers were considered very strong at that time.

In **1500** Swiss mercenaries stood on both sides. They served Duke **Ludovico Sforza** and also the French king. The mercenaries of Sforza refused to fight against their fellow countrymen. So Ludovico Sforza fell into **French captivity**. This is called the **“betrayal at Novara”**. In the same year **Bellinzona** with its three castles passed to Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden.

Cardinal **Matthäus Schiner**, Bishop of Sion, recruited Confederates against France on behalf of the Pope. In the **Pavia Expedition** of 1512 the Confederates drove the French out of Milan. They installed **Massimiliano Sforza**, the son of Ludovico, as duke. Milan was thus in effect a Confederate protectorate. In 1513 the Confederates defeated a French army at **Novara**.

In September **1515** the **Battle of Marignano** took place. The young French king **Francis I** had strong cavalry and many cannon. With the help of Venice he defeated the Confederates. **Ulrich Zwingli** was there as field preacher of the men of Glarus. His experiences later made him an opponent of mercenary service.

After Marignano the Confederates made **peace** with France in 1516. They gave up their plans for rule in northern Italy. But areas such as **Lugano** and **Locarno** remained in their possession. They were administered as **bailiwicks south of the Alps**. From these the canton of **Ticino** later developed.

gewusst: The three castles of Bellinzona are now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Marignano is often seen as the end of the Confederates' policy of conquest.

teile.einleitung: In the 19th century rich travellers discovered Switzerland. They came for the mountains and lakes. With the railway and big hotels tourism became an important branch of the economy.
wichtigste: In the 19th century especially many guests came from England.
The tourists wanted above all to see mountains and lakes.
Before the railway they travelled by stagecoach.
The railway brought more and more tourists.
Grand hotels offered the guests much luxury.
Around 1864 winter tourism began in St Moritz.
Thomas Cook led the first group tour through Switzerland in 1863.

abschnitte.text: In the past the Alps were thought eerie and dangerous. In the 18th and 19th centuries that changed. Poets and painters raved about the beauty of the mountains. Especially many guests came from **England**. They admired the **Alps**, the **glaciers** and the clear **lakes**. Some also wanted to climb the peaks themselves.

Before the railway tourists mostly travelled by **stagecoach** over the passes. That was slow and uncomfortable. With the **railway** one could travel much faster. So in the 19th century more and more tourists came to Switzerland. Soon **mountain railways** also went up, such as the railway up the Rigi in 1871. Many travellers had a red guidebook by **Karl Baedeker** with them. It described routes, hotels and sights.

For the rich guests big, splendid hotels were built. They are called **grand hotels**. They had many rooms, halls and often a lovely view. Such hotels stand, for example, in Lucerne, Interlaken or Montreux. Many people in the mountain villages found work there, as cooks, waiters or mountain guides.

For a long time guests came only in summer. Around **1864** the hotelier **Johannes Badrutt** invited English guests to come to **St Moritz** in winter. They liked staying, and so **winter tourism** began. In 1879 Badrutt had the first **electric light** in Switzerland installed in his Hotel Kulm. As early as 1863 the Englishman **Thomas Cook** had led a travel group through Switzerland. So began **package tourism**, in which everything is organised in advance.

gewusst: Badrutt is said to have promised the English guests to pay for their journey if they did not like the winter in St Moritz.
In 1857 the British founded the Alpine Club in London, the first alpine club in the world.

teile.einleitung: In the Uster Fire in 1832 home weavers set fire to a mechanical weaving mill in Oberuster. They were afraid of losing their work because of the new machines. The Uster Fire is the best known example of machine breaking in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Uster Fire happened on 22 November 1832.
It took place on the anniversary of the Uster Day of 1830.
The factory belonged to the firm Corrodi & Pfister.
Home weavers and small manufacturers were behind the deed.
They had earlier demanded a ban on power looms.
The ringleaders received harsh chain sentences in 1833.

abschnitte.text: In the Zurich Oberland many families lived from **home weaving**. They wove cloth at home on hand looms. Then **power looms** came along, driven by water power. These machines worked faster and more cheaply. The **home weavers** and small manufacturers, the so called **Tüchler**, feared for their livelihood. They saw in the machines the cause of falling wages.

On **22 November 1830** thousands of people had gathered in Uster. This **Uster Day** demanded a liberal constitution. The **Regeneration** in the canton of Zurich goes back to it, a period with more rights for the people. In the **Uster Memorial** the home workers also demanded a **ban on power looms**. The new liberal **Grand Council**, however, rejected this demand. That greatly disappointed the home weavers.

On **22 November 1832**, the anniversary of Uster Day, violence broke out. A crowd marched to the mechanical weaving mill in **Oberuster**. The factory belonged to the firm **Corrodi & Pfister**. It was set on fire and destroyed. Such violent destruction of machines out of fear for jobs is called **machine breaking**. In England too workers had destroyed looms.

After the fire a total of **75 people** were arrested. In 1833 the court gave its verdict. The ringleaders received harsh, **long chain sentences** in the penitentiary. The development could not be stopped, however. In the Zurich Oberland many **factories** arose in the following decades. The region became an important centre of the textile industry.

gewusst: The Uster Fire is the best known example of machine breaking in Switzerland.
The water power of the rivers early on made the Zurich Oberland a site for textile factories.

teile.einleitung: **Raetia** was a Roman province in the Alps and the Alpine foothills. The present-day Grisons also belonged to it. It was named after the **Rhaetians**, an Alpine people who lived there before the Romans.
wichtigste: Before the Romans, the Rhaetians lived in the Alpine valleys.
In 15 BC the Romans conquered the Alpine region as far as the Danube.
Drusus and Tiberius, the stepsons of Emperor Augustus, led the campaign.
The capital was Augusta Vindelicum, present-day Augsburg.
Around AD 300 Chur became the main town of Raetia prima.
Romansh developed from Vulgar Latin.

abschnitte.text: The **Rhaetians** were an Alpine people with their own **language** and **script**. They lived in the valleys of the present-day Grisons, Tyrol and northern Italy. In the Alpine foothills between Lake Constance and the Lech lived the **Vindelici**. So at the beginning the province was also called **“Raetia et Vindelicia”**.

Emperor **Augustus** wanted to secure the important **Alpine passes**. In **15 BC** his stepsons **Drusus** and **Tiberius** led a great campaign. Drusus marched from Italy over the Alps, Tiberius came from Lake Constance. In this way they enclosed the Alpine peoples from two sides. At **La Turbie** near Monaco the victory monument **Tropaeum Alpium** commemorates this. Its inscription lists 46 conquered Alpine peoples.

The capital of the province was **Augusta Vindelicum**, present-day **Augsburg**. The governor sat there. The province stretched from the Grisons to the **Danube**. In the east it bordered on **Noricum**, in the west on Germania Superior. Around AD 179 Raetia received its own legion, the **Legio III Italica**, whose camp was **Castra Regina** in present-day Regensburg.

Around **AD 300** Raetia was divided into two provinces. **Chur**, in Latin **Curia**, became the main town of the southern part, which was called **Raetia prima**. Later Chur also became a **bishop's seat**. Chur is therefore regarded as one of the oldest towns in Switzerland.

Over time the population adopted the **Vulgar Latin** of the Romans. Over many centuries **Romansh** developed from it. Today it is one of the four **national languages** of Switzerland and is spoken mainly in the Grisons.

gewusst: The word “Rhaeto-Romansh” still recalls the Rhaetians and the Roman province of Raetia.
The Tropaeum Alpium at La Turbie has been partly preserved to this day.

teile.einleitung: A villa rustica was a Roman country estate. In Roman times there were hundreds of such farms in the Swiss Plateau. They supplied cities and soldiers with food.
wichtigste: A villa rustica was a Roman agricultural estate.
The pars urbana was the owner's dwelling house.
The pars rustica was the working part with stables and workshops.
Some rooms had underfloor heating, the hypocaust.
The roofs were covered with fired tiles.
From about AD 260 raids by the Alemanni destroyed many estates.

abschnitte.text: After the Romans had conquered the area of present day Switzerland, many **estates** arose in the countryside. They are called **villa rustica**, which means “country house”. Such a farm included a dwelling house, **stables**, **granaries** and workshops. Often the whole was surrounded by a wall. In the **Swiss Plateau** there were hundreds of such estates.

A villa rustica had two parts. The **pars urbana** was the manor house in which the owner lived. It was often decorated with paintings and **mosaics**. The **pars rustica** was the working part with stables and workshops. The roofs were mostly covered with **fired tiles**. Flat flanged tiles and round curved tiles were combined.

Grand estates had **underfloor heating**, the **hypocaust**. A fire heated the air. The hot air flowed under the floor and through the walls. For this the floor rested on small **brick pillars**. Often there was also a **bath** of its own with warm and cold water.

The estates mainly grew **grain** and kept **livestock**. What they did not need themselves they sold to cities and to the **military**. The estate of **Orbe-Boscéaz** in the canton of Vaud is known for its coloured **floor mosaics**. They show, for example, gods and animals. Around **AD 260** the **Alemanni** pushed across the Rhine and plundered. Many estates were destroyed or abandoned.

gewusst: The Romans brought roof tiles of fired clay to our region; before that roofs were mostly covered with straw or wood.
Many place names in Switzerland go back to Roman estates.

tszy6ib.t: The watch industry in the Jura

teile.einleitung: The Jura is the heart of Swiss watchmaking. There farming families used to make watch parts in winter. Later factories and whole towns arose for the watchmakers.
wichtigste: Huguenots from France brought knowledge of watchmaking to Geneva in the 16th century.
In the Etablissage home workers made individual watch parts.
The World's Fair of 1876 in Philadelphia shocked the Swiss watchmakers.
La Chaux-de-Fonds was rebuilt in a chessboard pattern after a fire.
Watchmakers' houses have many large windows.
Saint-Imier in the Bernese Jura is a watchmaking centre.
The balance wheel sets the beat in a mechanical watch.

abschnitte.text: In the 16th century many **Huguenots** fled from France to Geneva. They were Reformed refugees for their faith. They brought a great deal of craft skill with them. Because Calvin strictly limited jewellery, goldsmiths turned to watchmaking. From Geneva the craft later spread into the **Jura**.

In the Jura many **farming families** worked at home on watch parts in winter. Each family often made only one particular part. This system is called the **Etablissage**. The **Etablisseur** collected the parts, had them assembled and sold the finished watches. For the tiny parts good light was needed. That is why old watchmakers' houses have strikingly many large **windows**, with the workbenches standing right in front of them.

In **1794** a great fire destroyed large parts of **La Chaux-de-Fonds**. In the rebuilding straight, wide streets were laid out in a **chessboard pattern**. The houses were built so that a lot of daylight came in. In **Saint-Imier** in the Bernese Jura too a centre of watch manufacture arose in the 19th century. Saint-Imier belongs to the canton of **Bern**.

At the **World's Fair of 1876 in Philadelphia** Swiss visitors saw American factories. These made watches cheaply with machines. After that the Swiss watch industry was strongly **mechanised**. Inside every mechanical wristwatch or pocket watch the **balance wheel** swings evenly back and forth. It regulates the running of the watch. In big pendulum clocks a **pendulum** takes over this task.

gewusst: A mechanical wristwatch often consists of over a hundred individual parts.
The balance wheel in many wristwatches swings back and forth several times a second.

teile.einleitung: On 21 June 1339 **Bern** and its allies fought at **Laupen** against Fribourg and many nobles of western Switzerland. Bern won the battle. The victory strengthened the city and its link with the forest cantons.
wichtigste: The Battle of Laupen took place on 21 June 1339.
Bern came to the aid of the besieged castle of Laupen.
Its opponents were Fribourg and the nobility of western Switzerland.
Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden helped Bern.
According to Konrad Justinger, Rudolf von Erlach led the Bernese.
In 1340 Agnes of Hungary mediated peace.

abschnitte.text: In the 14th century **Bern** grew ever stronger and acquired a lot of land. The city of **Fribourg** and the **nobility of western Switzerland** feared this growing power. There was also a dispute with the emperor: Bern did not want to recognise **Louis the Bavarian** because he was under the **excommunication** of the Pope. This sharpened the conflict.

The little town of **Laupen** on the Sense belonged to Bern. Its opponents besieged it with a large army. Bern gathered allies. **Uri**, **Schwyz** and **Unterwalden** sent warriors, and **Solothurn** and some valley communities helped too. On **21 June 1339** the army marched to relieve the besieged.

Bern and its allies **won** the battle. According to the chronicler **Konrad Justinger**, the Bernese knight **Rudolf von Erlach** led the army. Justinger, however, wrote his chronicle only many decades later. In Bern a **monument** commemorates Rudolf von Erlach.

After the battle the war went on for a while. In **1340** **Agnes of Hungary** mediated peace. She was a **Habsburg** and lived in **Königsfelden Abbey** in Aargau. Agnes was a respected mediator in many disputes. Bern was able to build up its position further afterwards and joined the Confederation in 1353.

gewusst: The little town of Laupen lies where the Sense flows into the Saane.
Laupen is now in the canton of Bern, close to the border with the canton of Fribourg.

teile.einleitung: On 25 July 1940 General Henri Guisan gathered the senior officers of the Swiss army on the **Rütli meadow**. This meeting is called the **Rütli Report** (Rütlirapport). Guisan wanted to show that Switzerland would defend itself against an attack.
wichtigste: The Rütli Report took place on 25 July 1940.
About 650 officers of the rank of major and above took part.
France had capitulated to Germany shortly before.
Switzerland was almost completely surrounded by Germany and Italy.
Guisan explained the new strategy of the Réduit in the Alps.
The officers travelled by boat across the Urnersee.

abschnitte.text: In the Second World War Germany had defeated **France** in June 1940. Now Switzerland was almost completely enclosed by the **Axis powers**, that is, by Germany and Italy. Many people in Switzerland were uncertain. Some doubted whether resistance still made sense at all. General **Henri Guisan** wanted to strengthen the will to defend the country.

Guisan deliberately chose the **Rütli** on the **Urnersee**. According to tradition, the alliance of the Confederates was sworn there. About **650 officers** of the rank of major and above came together on **25 July 1940**. The Rütli can only be reached on foot or by **boat**, and the officers too travelled across the lake.

Guisan explained the new defence strategy: the **Réduit**. In an attack the army was to withdraw into the **Alps** and defend itself there. The important Alpine passes and tunnels were not to fall into foreign hands. This was meant to make an attack on Switzerland very costly for any enemy.

Guisan gave his speech **largely off the cuff** and not exactly according to his manuscript. The well-known version of the speech was only revised later. The meeting was also dangerous: **almost the entire army leadership** was in one place. An attack could have left the army without leadership at a stroke. Even so, Guisan stuck to this symbolic meeting.

gewusst: The officers travelled to the Rütli on the steamship “Stadt Luzern”, which still sails on Lake Lucerne today.
The Rütli meadow was bought in 1859 with donations from all over Switzerland, and schoolchildren also collected for it; it was then given to the Confederation.

teile.einleitung: Swiss chocolate is known all over the world. In the 19th century pioneers founded the first factories and invented new processes. Especially important was the invention of milk chocolate in Vevey.
wichtigste: In 1819 François-Louis Cailler founded one of the first mechanised chocolate factories near Vevey.
Philippe Suchard founded his factory in Serrières near Neuchâtel in 1826.
The Zurich Sprüngli family began making chocolate in 1845.
In 1875 Daniel Peter developed a milk chocolate in Vevey that could be made industrially.
Henri Nestlé helped him with his experience of milk products.
Switzerland had plenty of milk, while cocoa and sugar had to be imported.

abschnitte.text: In 1819 **François-Louis Cailler** founded one of the first mechanised chocolate factories in Switzerland in Corsier near **Vevey**. In 1826 **Philippe Suchard** followed in **Serrières** near Neuchâtel. He used **water power** for his machines. The Lake Geneva region became a centre of chocolate making.

Chocolate was also made in German-speaking Switzerland. The Zurich confectioner family **Sprüngli** began making solid chocolate in 1845. The family ran a **confiserie** in Zurich, that is, a shop for fine sweets. Their production later grew into a well-known chocolate company.

**Daniel Peter** was a trained candle maker. In 1863 he married Cailler's eldest daughter and so came to chocolate. He wanted to combine cocoa with milk. The problem was the **water** in the milk, which made the chocolate go bad. In 1875 in Vevey he succeeded in making a milk chocolate that could be produced in factories. He was helped by his friend **Henri Nestlé**, who made baby food from milk in Vevey.

In the 19th century Swiss farming specialised strongly in **dairy farming**. So there was plenty of fresh milk. **Cocoa** and **sugar**, on the other hand, do not grow in Switzerland and had to be imported. The combination of Swiss milk with imported cocoa made milk chocolate a typically Swiss product.

The Swiss chocolate factories soon sold their products in many countries. Some well-known brands from that time still exist today. Switzerland is among the countries where the most chocolate is eaten per person. Chocolate is also an important **export product** and a souvenir for tourists.

gewusst: Daniel Peter, the inventor of industrial milk chocolate, was actually a candle maker.
Cocoa trees grow only in warm countries near the equator, never in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In Swiss history, Regeneration is the name for the period from 1830 to 1848. At that time many cantons gave themselves new, liberal constitutions in which the people, and no longer a small upper class, held power. The Regeneration was an important step on the road to the modern federal state of 1848.
wichtigste: The Regeneration lasted roughly from 1830 to 1848.
The impulse came from the July Revolution in France in 1830.
Ticino gave itself a liberal constitution even before the July Revolution.
The new cantonal constitutions established the principle of popular sovereignty.
The Uster Day of 22 November 1830 was a great popular assembly of the Zurich countryside.
In 1833 the canton of Basel was divided after fierce conflicts between city and countryside.
In the spirit of the Regeneration the University of Zurich was founded in 1833.

abschnitte.text: The word **Regeneration** means renewal. After the Restoration from 1814 to 1830, a few wealthy families had once again ruled in many cantons. The **liberals** wanted to change this and demanded freedom and equality for all citizens. From 1830 they pushed through new constitutions in many cantons.

In July 1830 the people of Paris overthrew their king Charles X in the **July Revolution**. This news encouraged many people in Switzerland too. Ticino, however, had already given itself a liberal constitution before the July Revolution. Zurich, Bern, Lucerne, Aargau, Thurgau, St Gallen and Solothurn, among others, followed.

On 22 November 1830 thousands of people from the Zurich countryside met in Uster for the **Uster Day**. They demanded a new constitution in which the countryside would count as much as the city of Zurich. An important programme paper of the Zurich liberals was the **Küssnacht Memorial** by Ludwig Snell. Soon afterwards Zurich got a new constitution.

The regenerated constitutions established **popular sovereignty**, that is, rule by the people. This included equality before the law, freedom of the press and the separation of powers. The cantons also expanded the primary school so that all children learned to read and write. In 1833 the University of Zurich was founded, followed in 1834 by the University of Bern.

Not everyone agreed with the innovations. In the canton of Basel there was fierce fighting between city and countryside, and in 1833 the canton was divided into **Basel-Stadt** and Basel-Landschaft. In 1832 seven liberal cantons joined together in the **Siebnerkonkordat** (Concordat of Seven). The conservative cantons responded with the **Sarnerbund** (Sarnen League).

abschnitte.titel: On the way to the federal state
abschnitte.text: The Rossi Plan of 1832 and 1833 was meant to renew the federal treaty but found no majority in the cantons. In 1839 the appointment of the theologian David Friedrich Strauss to Zurich led to the **Züriputsch**, in which the liberals there lost power. Tensions between liberals and conservatives continued to grow. They finally led to the Sonderbund War of 1847 and to the Federal Constitution of 1848.

begriffe.erklaerung: The basic law of a state, which sets out the most important rules and rights.
The principle that all power in the state comes from the people.
A political movement that demanded freedom, equality and a say for citizens.
A sudden, usually violent overthrow of a government.

gewusst: The word “Putsch” spread throughout the German-speaking world through the Zurich coup of 1839.
Since the division of 1833 there have been two cantons of Basel, which are still separate today.
About 10,000 people are said to have gathered at the Uster Day, a huge number for that time.

teile.einleitung: In September 1798 French troops attacked the small canton of Nidwalden. The people of Nidwalden had refused to recognise the new Helvetic Constitution. The fighting went down in history as the “Terror Days of Nidwalden”.
wichtigste: In 1798 the Helvetic Republic was created under French influence.
Nidwalden refused to swear the oath to the Helvetic Constitution.
Father Paul Styger called for resistance; the Landsgemeinde followed him on 29 August 1798.
From 7 to 9 September 1798 General Schauenburg attacked with about 10,000 men.
About 400 people of Nidwalden died; Stansstad, Buochs and Ennetmoos were destroyed.
Heinrich Pestalozzi afterwards looked after war orphans in Stans.

abschnitte.text: In spring 1798 French troops occupied the Old Confederation. France established the **Helvetic Republic**, a unitary state with a common constitution. The old states lost their independence. All citizens were to swear an **oath of allegiance** to the new constitution. Many people in central Switzerland refused, because they saw their old rights and their faith threatened.

Resistance was especially strong in Nidwalden. The Capuchin friar **Paul Styger** urged the population to resist. On 29 August 1798 the **Landsgemeinde** rejected the constitution and refused the oath. For the government of the Helvetic Republic and for France this was an open rebellion. So they decided to subdue Nidwalden by force.

The French general **Balthasar von Schauenburg** had already defeated Bern. With about 10,000 soldiers he attacked Nidwalden from several sides, over land and over Lake Lucerne. The fighting lasted from 7 to 9 September 1798. 9 September was the worst day. The people of Nidwalden were far outnumbered and could not stop the attack.

About **400 people** lost their lives, including women and children. **Stansstad**, Buochs and Ennetmoos were completely destroyed. In all of Nidwalden about 600 houses burned down. Many families lost their homes and their belongings. For the small canton this was one of the greatest catastrophes in its history.

After the fighting there were many children without parents. The Helvetic government asked **Heinrich Pestalozzi** to run an orphanage in **Stans**.
